InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Rebuilds the Copilot App's Diff Surface to Open Million-Line Pull Requests Without Jank.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub engineering has published a detailed account of how it rebuilt the diff surface in the GitHub Copilot app to open a pull request with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines and more than 400 inline review comments without turning the review into a waiting exercise.

The post, by Principal Design Engineer Alberto Gimeno, lands at a moment when AI coding agents are producing far more pull requests than reviewers can digest, and the bottleneck has moved from writing code to reading it.

At the heart of the rebuild is a decision to stop pretending a pull request is a single uniform list. Code rows have a known height at a known font size, so their geometry can be computed up front and never rebuilt. Comments do not. A markdown body wraps differently at different widths, sections can be toggled in place, reply composers grow as a user types, and images change height when they load. Rather than force one variable-height virtualizer to absorb both, the team split the document into two independent domains:.

Dynamic blocks are keyed by identity (file, line, side) rather than pixel position, with a fingerprint tracking content, open state and measurement width. A single idle-gated measurement pass reads mounted blocks in one batch, scoped to roughly 2,400 pixels around the viewport, and corrections are anchored to whatever the reader is looking at so the surface never fights an active scroll.

Gimeno is open about an early mistake, the team's first instinct was one ResizeObserver per block writing heights back into the layout, a classic feedback loop whose cost grows with every mounted block. The shipped design keeps the observer but defaults it to flagging rather than writing, with a deliberate frame-synchronous exception when the user toggles a or expands a reply composer, so the code below moves in the same frame.

The work builds on an April 2026 post from the main github.com files-changed team, who reported that unified-view diff lines previously rendered as roughly eight React components and ten DOM elements each, and cut both roughly in half.

GitHub's own stacked pull requests went into public preview on 30 July 2026 as an explicit answer to AI-generated monsters, and a DEV Community piece cited Microsoft research finding review quality degrades sharply once a pull request exceeds roughly 200 lines, a rounding error against the Copilot app's million-line test case.

Third-party tools have filled the gap from the review side. Graphite, Pullfrog and CodeRabbit each take different runs at agent-era review, with Codegen CEO Jay Hack arguing that the winners in this fresh era will be the teams that redesign their workflows around the fact that review, not code, is now the bottleneck.

It has been revealed that the team also describes the measurement loop built around the rebuild. The surface carries permanent structured probes for its own invariants, which run as CI budgets against a synthetic huge-pull-request fixture, and an autopilot drives the real desktop app through a scripted flow, cold and warm, so an agent can read the on-disk log and spot regressions without anyone at the keyboard. Gimeno's closing line is addressed to anyone who reviews code for a living: open the worst pull request you have got.

The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.

In a recent development, while Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the tech giant's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:.

It has been revealed that the scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.

Sources indicate that at some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

Newly introduced research has warned companies looking to replace human workers with AI could face major reputational consequences later on down the line if their AI strategies fall apart.

Companies that are forced to re-hire human workers after laying them off could ultimately find themselves having to pay higher salaries, offer better contractual terms and include stronger employment protections, the report from JobAssist warns.

But even after offering workers better terms overall, they could have already made reputational and loyalty damages – nearly one-third (29%) of workers say they'd return to their old job, but would immediately start looking for another.

It has been revealed that while a relatively low but not insignificant number of workers would likely continue to look for other opportunities, the number of workers looking for a higher salary (71%) is much higher. Nearly two in three (64%) also said they'd negotiate more aggressively in general when returning to an old job.

Sources indicate that however, workers are still very clearly worried about AI's impacts on their roles, because half (54%) would now prioritize job security over titles and perks, implying they're concerned about experiencing yet another redundancy. Nearly half (44%) also stated they'd trust their employer less after AI replaced human workers.

All in all, the study is proof that employer reputation could suffer beyond the original workforce reduction, with laid off workers and re-hires less likely to trust the company.

And even after all the costs associated with laying off workers in the first place, and investing so heavily in artificial intelligence, JobAssist warns that workers could end up demanding more money, benefits and security than they had done before.

"For businesses evaluating the financial benefits of replacing employees with AI, the survey highlights a risk that could emerge if an automation decision has to be reversed," the report summarized.

#565. AI Is Only as Smart as the Financial Data Behind It

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite

AI Is Only as Smart as the Financial Data Behind It

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI has become part of almost every conversation about the future of finance.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve spent my career building and scaling payments infrastructure, and the hardest problems have rarely been the algorithms.
  • The challenge is especially visible in finance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI has become part of almost every conversation about the future of finance. Organizations are investing in AI to automate routine work, improve forecasting and help employees make faster decisions. Most of those conversations start with models and applications. In my experience, they should start with the quality, connectivity and governance of the data those systems rely on.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent my career building and scaling payments infrastructure, and the hardest problems have rarely been the algorithms. They’ve been the underlying infrastructure needed for accounting platforms, banks, payroll providers and payment rails to describe the same business event the same way.

The challenge is especially visible in finance. Accounting, banking, payroll, invoicing and payments all generate information that shapes business decisions. When those systems operate independently, they create fragmented data environments that make it much harder for AI to establish context across the organization. AI can identify patterns within individual systems, but it cannot reliably explain what is happening across the business without a connected view of an organization’s finances. Early on at Melio, we ran into a version of this that sounds trivial and isn’t: what does “paid” mean? A customer approves a payment on Monday. Funds leave their account Tuesday. The vendor’s bank makes them available Thursday. The transaction gets matched to an invoice the following week. Four timestamps, four defensible answers to “when was this paid,” none of them wrong. A human accountant works around that ambiguity without thinking about it. A forecasting model that treats “paid date” as a single field produces predictions that are confidently and systematically wrong about timing — which is the one thing cash flow forecasting has to get right. Connecting those systems was the necessary first step. Getting them to agree on what the fields meant is what made the connection worth anything. In finance, “AI-ready” starts with connected, and connected only counts when the systems describe the same event the same way.

The need for connected financial data is becoming more urgent. Xero’s Small Business Insights report found that U.S. small businesses now wait an average of 29.3 days to be paid, while annual sales growth of 4.0% remains below its long-term average. When payment timing, expenses and demand all move independently, organizations need systems capable of connecting those signals rather than analyzing each in isolation — and that’s as true for a large enterprise’s treasury operation as it is for a 10-person business.

Sources indicate that consider a business deciding whether it can hire another employee before the end of the quarter. That decision depends on more than today’s bank balance: expected customer payments, payroll commitments, recurring expenses, upcoming tax obligations and projected revenue all factor in. No single metric provides a reliable answer. Bringing those inputs together gives leaders a clearer understanding of their financial position and gives AI something meaningful to reason over. Automation requires access to transactions. Reasoning requires context.

It has been revealed that finance teams can spend the first part of every month reconciling data across systems before meaningful analysis begins. By the time they have a complete picture, the cash flow change they are trying to understand may already be weeks old. That lag is precisely what connected data can reduce.

The first generation of AI in finance focused on efficiency: categorizing transactions, processing invoices, helping teams complete routine tasks faster. Those capabilities still deliver value, but expectations are shifting from task automation toward context-aware decision support — earlier visibility into cash flow risks, better forecast accuracy, and an understanding of how changes in payment behavior, expenses or revenue patterns could affect future performance.

Sources indicate that delivering that requires AI to analyze financial data in context. The meaning of any transaction depends on the conditions around it: an increase in expenses could indicate overspending or reflect inventory purchases ahead of seasonal demand; a decline in cash reserves could signal liquidity pressure or simply the timing of quarterly tax payments. AI becomes valuable when it can do the same — connecting patterns across historical transactions, cash positions, receivables and operational signals to distinguish a meaningful shift from a routine fluctuation.

According to recent reports, for technology leaders evaluating AI in finance, the consequential question is not which application to deploy first, but whether the underlying data environment can provide the complete and timely context those applications require. When building these systems, a few investments matter most:.

Recent findings suggest that treat integrations as contracts, not connections. A one-time sync between an accounting platform and a payments system will drift. Define explicit data contracts — schemas, field definitions, freshness guarantees — so that when an upstream system changes, downstream AI doesn’t silently degrade.

It has been revealed that move from batch reconciliation to event-driven data flows. If financial data is reconciled weekly or monthly, AI is forecasting from stale information. Event-driven pipelines that propagate transactions as they happen give models the currency they need to detect changes early.

Industry observers note that establish a semantic layer for financial metrics. “Cash position,” “outstanding receivables” and “revenue” must mean the same thing in every system. Without consistent definitions, AI will confidently produce answers that no two teams interpret the same way.

It has been revealed that evaluate AI outputs against ground truth. The ledger is finance’s advantage over most AI domains: there is a verifiable record. AI-generated financial insights should be held to the same standard as a junior analyst’s work, tested against actuals, with accuracy measured over time. Trust in AI recommendations is earned through measurement, not asserted.

These investments attract less attention than the AI applications built on top of them, but they determine whether those applications work.

As AI becomes embedded in financial management, the technical challenge is shifting from what individual models can do to how effectively they operate within the broader financial data architecture.

Organizations that invest in connected data will identify cash flow changes earlier and have greater confidence in AI-generated forecasts. The difference isn’t the model. It’s the data behind it.

Following the exit of Nvidia's CEO last week, a petition has been put together to campaign for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang.

VideoCardz noticed the 'Stand with Jensen' website which hosts a petition and open letter that has now been signed by some 175,000 people, some of whom are high-profile names in the tech industry.

In a recent development, that includes Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney (of Epic Games), Tobias Lutke (CEO of Shopify), Travis Kalanick (the former CEO of Uber), Steve Chen (the former CTO of YouTube) and Julien Chaumond (current CTO at Hugging Face). It's made clear that Huang himself doesn't endorse the letter.

The demands laid out by the letter to the Nvidia board are threefold, including firstly that Huang should be reinstated as CEO immediately – to stabilize the situation – but if the board believes "his continued absence is necessary" that they should provide an explanation of why.

The second demand is to "ensure an independent investigation and a fair hearing", and the third is to deliver a timely public explanation of what's happened and how the interests of Nvidia staff and shareholders were weighed up in this matter.

It has been revealed that the petition states: "Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.".

In a recent development, meanwhile, given all this, a separate report from The Financial Times claims that Huang is mulling a comeback bid and the "possibility of returning" based on chatter from multiple sources. An ally of the ex-CEO noted they were putting together a 'war room' of significant tech executives to lobby for Huang's return (presumably including Musk and the other aforementioned names).

Some strong feelings have been aired, then, and based on the stats from the Stand with Jensen campaign, nearly 9,000 Nvidia staff (known as 'Nvidians') are signatories of the open letter – which is 20% of the employee base. Of those employees, 26 are Vice Presidents (or Senior VPs), which is a good chunk of the top leadership (maybe approaching half of them, although there are no precise numbers for VPs at Team Green).

Of course, none of this can be verified, and we have to take these numbers on trust.

Looking at Reddit, there's little sympathy for Huang, particularly among PC gamers (though his exit is arguably another distinctly negative development). Even on the subreddits relating to Nvidia stock, there's a mostly dim view of this petition (just over half of the signatories are declared as shareholders). However, it is notable that a fair few major names in tech have signed the letter – I still doubt that this will spark a turnaround in sentiment for the board, of course. These kind of campaigns aren't known for producing much in the way of concrete results, shall we say.

Sources indicate that that said, given the 'war room' rumor from the FT, maybe the petition will give Huang a bit more impetus to launch the comeback bid that is supposedly being considered behind the scenes. If it's going to happen, it will obviously need to happen swiftly.

Meanwhile, the letter signatures are likely to exceed 200,000 today. In case you missed this last week (somehow), Colette Kress (who was CFO) is currently the interim CEO while Nvidia conducts a search for Huang's permanent replacement (who could come from inside or outside the firm).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.
  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services. AWS Emulator lets developers and coding agents create resources, hit the same errors AWS would return, and iterate without provisioning cloud resources or incurring service charges for the operations it emulates.

Teams point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at it with environment variables such as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, leaving application code unchanged. On Linux it installs as an RPM or Debian package for x86_64 or aarch64; on macOS and Windows, AWS documents a short Dockerfile and does not publish a prebuilt image. Rust tests can use an embedded mode that runs the emulator inside the test process and wires its HTTP client into the AWS SDK for Rust. An aws-emulator skill can start the emulator for coding agents and check a project against published fidelity tests. Written in Rust, it is generated from more than 400 Smithy API models AWS publishes for the SDKs, according to Swaminathan Sivasubramanian.

AWS states agents wrote and tested the code. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, describes three teams: one writes fidelity tests from the public API models and verifies them against real AWS, one replays those tests and files concerns, and one implements each fix. Every change must pass a merge gate that checks compilation, coding standards, security, and fidelity regressions. The work runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit.

According to recent reports, how closely the emulator matches AWS varies by service. AWS publishes versioned fidelity tests and per-service scores with each release; a test passes only when every call matches AWS, including status codes, side effects, and exact errors. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 with the error code NotImplemented. AWS states fidelity is closest on control-plane APIs, while data-plane behavior and support for CloudFormation, Terraform, and the AWS CDK vary by service. Documented limits include no evaluation of IAM or resource-based policies, so it must not be used to test security; a single shared account and Region per process; in-memory state that disappears when the process stops; and no testing for long-running use or load. The evaluation suite includes tests the emulator does not yet pass.

It has been revealed that developers already have several local AWS stand-ins, including LocalStack, Floci, and moto. AWS Emulator is generated from AWS's own API models, ships official fidelity scores, and is dedicated to the public domain, but it is not a drop-in replacement for every workflow those tools cover, especially permission testing and infrastructure-as-code pipelines.

According to recent reports, AWS just released a free local emulator of its APIs, made for coding agents and written entirely by agents. I counted its published fidelity tests: S3, DynamoDB and SQS pass about 2 in 3. CloudFormation passes under 1 in 5.

Yurii Serhiichuk compared it with existing emulators and published a container image and GitHub Action to cover a packaging gap:.

According to recent reports, AWS shipped AWS Emulator today - think LocalStack/Floci but native. Rust, built by agents (so hopefully it gets updated pretty fast). No public docker image though, and no GitHub action. So I filled that part.

  • It has been revealed that claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both customers and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5.
  • It has been revealed that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load.
  • In a recent development, building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both customers and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden, in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here.

It has been revealed that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space.

In a recent development, building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass.

Industry observers note that likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering.

The result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now. As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language.

The demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive.

Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author states that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB.

Regular computing users, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the "demoscene.".

By no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes.

Hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004.

#560. North America and UK are among worst for indoor mobile signal, study finds

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (539 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

North America and UK are among worst for indoor mobile signal, study finds

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume.
  • Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania.
  • But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume.

Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania.

But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong. According to Ookla, the material a building is constructed from can make a difference to a signal’s ability to pass through walls, but it’s not a dramatic difference, with timber-framed buildings reducing a signal by 2 dB (decibels), while concrete ones still only drop it by 7 dB, with the median drop being 4 dB.

That accounts for under a tenth of the overall difference in indoor signal between different cities and regions, with 85% of the difference coming from how good the outdoor signal is. So in other words, cities with better outdoor signal tend to have better indoor signal, too — which isn't entirely surprising.

These differences are surprisingly big, with the median indoor signal measured in the likes of Dubai, Bangkok, and Seoul being around -88 dBm (decibel-milliwatts) on 4G, whereas in Naples it’s -105 dBm and in Geneva and Birmingham it’s -104 dBm. Numbers closer to zero are better here, and that roughly -17 dBm gap is a difference of around 50 times in signal power.

Overall, North American cities have a median signal of -101 dBm, with European ones similarly posting a median of -100 dBm, while in for example East Asia the median is -90 dBm — making for a much better signal.

So even though your signal might not seem bad outside, it likely is if you’re getting poor indoor signal — it’s just the move to indoors decreases it ever further, making it more noticeable.

The solution is for carriers to rethink their network deployment, with for example a denser deployment of masts and other infrastructure, or the use of more or better configured spectrum.

Still, without changes at a government level, this probably won’t be addressed, with Ookla noting that cities and countries that have indoor-specific rules for coverage tend to perform better than those that don’t.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has been rumored to be launching an AI-powered Health+ app for over a year now — and while that still hasn’t emerged, the company has just debuted an ‘Apple Health AI Study App’ that could be laying the groundwork for something bigger.

Sources indicate that this new app has been made in collaboration with OpenEvidence — a leading clinical AI platform — and it’s designed to help the two companies explore how AI can be used in healthcare. According to the App Store description, it will also “help Apple build better health AI products.”.

That means it could be a stepping stone towards Health+ or other AI health tools from Apple — but in the meantime, this app sounds potentially very useful itself.

You can ask the app questions about your conditions or symptoms, and you’ll get responses in “approachable language,” complete with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations, so that you don’t have to just blindly take the AI’s word for something.

You can also optionally share HealthKit data such as your resting heart rate, activity, and sleep, to give the app more context, and you can use this to prepare for a medical visit, or to build personalized exercise and meal looks.

The AI here has been trained on peer-reviewed medical research and clinical guidelines, so hopefully its responses will be more reliable than those from a standard AI chatbot, though a disclaimer notes that “neither the app nor the research study provides medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.”.

However, Apple does promise to protect your privacy with this app — while it’s intended for research, your responses won’t be used to train AI models, and you can also choose what to share, with Apple claiming that it will protect the confidentiality of your information.

NEA led the round, with continued participation from Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue, bringing Corma’s total funding to $185 million.

Corma stated the new capital would accelerate scaling of its foundation models, expand compute capacity and support selective hiring. The Series A follows its emergence from stealth on August 10, 2026 with $60 million in seed funding.

The company characterized demand from the world’s largest organizations as overwhelming and identified securing enough compute for that demand and its waitlist as one of its central challenges. Corma’s ability to expand access therefore depends on obtaining additional infrastructure as well as advancing its models.

It has been revealed that the company deploys those models through the Corma Workforce, a system designed to work autonomously alongside human security teams. It operates within customers’ existing security and IT stacks, including identity, cloud, endpoint, security information and event management, and firewall or intrusion-detection tools. Its work spans investigations, connecting evidence and taking action across those systems.

Employees can assign tasks through Slack or Teams, ask questions, review findings and approve actions. The design adds AI-led execution to a customer’s current operating environment while keeping human review in the workflow.

Corma reports live deployments across healthcare, finance, energy, critical infrastructure and retail, with 99% of security tasks completed autonomously and successfully, 100 times faster end-to-end completion and 95% lower cost per completed task.

One anonymized Fortune 1000 services-organization CISO quoted on the product page remarked end-to-end response time fell 94% in a comparison with the customer’s former service provider, which the customer subsequently replaced with Corma.

Corma’s launch statement argues that improvements in coding and software reasoning map more directly to offensive security than to the broader defensive workload. Vulnerability research and exploit development are code-reasoning problems against bounded targets; defense instead requires continuous analysis of audit logs, events, configurations and network flows. It also involves connecting weak signals across systems and long periods while making thousands of accurate, consistent decisions each day under changing conditions.

That distinction is the basis for Corma’s focus on domain-specific foundation models. Its stated development program includes rethinking model architecture, extending context to detect faint anomaly signals, adversarial self-play and continuous learning that can establish baselines over months and years.

CEO Alon Pluda and the Corma team said the next generation of its foundation models would be shared soon, without giving a release date. The financing supports that next phase of model development and selective hiring, but the immediate scaling constraint is compute: broader deployments require enough additional capacity to serve current demand and organizations on the waitlist.

It's hard to ignore all the chatter around Claude lately. I have been a long-time Gemini user on Android, and while it's served me well, all the praise surrounding Claude finally got to me.

I decided to see what the fuss was about and replaced Gemini with Claude as my main AI assistant on Android.

While Claude delivered on several fronts, I didn't anticipate how much I would miss some of Gemini's everyday conveniences.

Gemini has been my default AI assistant on Android for quite some time, and I never had any major complaints about it.

Google's deep ecosystem integration made it convenient.

It has been revealed that however, I wasn't always impressed with the quality of its responses. Sometimes, Gemini's answers felt overly structured, generic, or unnecessarily robotic, especially when I needed help with writing, brainstorming, or complex topics.

I wasn't fond of Google's confusing lineup of AI models and the way some of its most capable features were tied to expensive subscriptions.

Meanwhile, Claude was receiving plenty of attention for its conversational abilities, coding capabilities, and productivity features.

Since I regularly use AI for research, brainstorming, and managing projects, I wanted to see whether those strengths would make a meaningful difference on my phone.

The difference became apparent within my first few conversations.

It has been revealed that claude felt like a refreshing change. Its answers were more natural, thoughtful, and engaging.

Instead of throwing information at me, Claude seemed to understand the intent behind my questions.

I enjoyed using it to brainstorm article ideas, refine headlines, and discuss complex topics.

Industry observers note that another area where Claude impressed me was writing. Whether I needed a different perspective on a topic or help simplifying a technical explanation, its suggestions often required fewer adjustments.

Gemini is no slouch here, but Claude's conversational style felt more aligned with how I prefer to work.

I initially expected Claude's Android app to be little more than a basic chatbot interface. Thankfully, I was wrong.

The app has a clean, distraction-free design that puts conversations front and center.

Sources indicate that voice mode is another welcome addition. I can have natural conversations with Claude, switch between text and voice, and continue discussing ideas when I don't feel like typing.

Claude also supports Projects where I can keep all the context in one place and start asking questions.

Recent findings suggest that it even has a Scheduled section to automate tasks. Overall, Claude is more capable than I initially expected.

But as I moved past normal conversations, cracks started to appear in my workflow.

Sources indicate that that's when I started questioning my decision to switch. Don't get me wrong, Claude has an impressive collection of connectors.

It works with Gmail, Google Drive, Google Calendar, and various third-party services like Airtable, Figma, and more.

That's fantastic when I am working on complex projects, but these aren't necessarily the integrations I care about most when using an AI assistant on my phone.

My everyday Android workflow revolves around apps like YouTube Music, Google Photos, WhatsApp, Google Keep, and other mobile-friendly services.

With Gemini, I can ask it to find pictures from my Vietnam trip, play my favorite playlist, retrieve information from my notes, create newly introduced tasks, or help me draft and send a message on WhatsApp.

I don't have to constantly switch between apps to get things done.

Claude supports basic Android actions, but it lacks the same depth of integration with my favorite mobile apps.

I can't search my Google Photos library or control YouTube Music the way Gemini can.

It has been revealed that that's what frustrated me most. I appreciate having access to hundreds of professional integrations, but on Android, I need support for the apps I use daily.

This was another trade-off that surprised me. Gemini isn't just a chatbot for me.

It's also a handy creative tool I frequently use to generate images, edit existing pictures, and experiment with AI videos.

Google's Nano Banana image generator is impressive. Whether I need a quick social media poster, want to change the background of a family photo, or have a creative idea, I can get the job done without leaving Gemini.

Claude can analyze uploaded images and help me brainstorm creative ideas; it doesn't offer native AI image generation or photo editing.

I can ask it to write a detailed image prompt, but I still need another app to bring that idea to life.

After spending an entire month with Claude on Android, I have an appreciation for what Anthropic has built.

Claude impressed me with its responses and powerful productivity features, but in many areas, I preferred Gemini.

Claude is an excellent chatbot, but Gemini feels like a complete Android assistant.

So, after a month of testing, I am moving back to Gemini as my default assistant.

Zimperium’s zLabs team has published latest research on ArcticRAT. For those of you who are not familiar, ArcticRAT is an Android remote access trojan that has evolved into an AI-powered, full device-takeover tool.

Industry observers note that the malware is now capable of sending stolen SMS messages and app data to a commercial large language model (LLM) to determine target victims’ financial standing. Needless to say, this makes it a lot more dangerous.

In a recent development, AI has essentially been added to the attack chain, unfortunately. Prompts that are sent to an LLM API actually filter stolen SMS messages for one-time passcodes, balance changes, and transfer notices.

On top of that, they estimate each victim’s financial standing. Based on that, targets are being identified. Zimperium notes that this was first seen in samples from mid-July this year.

ArcticRAT can take full control of your phone. The device can look switched off to its owner, but the attacker is essentially using it. The attacker can move through the victim’s banking apps, watch the screen, listen in through the microphone, and log every keystroke.

There’s also the fake lock screen that steals PINs, patterns, and passwords, plus Wireless Debugging (ADB) abuse that can strip the lock screen or lock the owner out of the phone.

Industry observers note that needless to say, Zimperium went into a lot more technical details in the full report, but this is the gist of it. ArcticRAT is now far more capable than it was before, and thanks to the AI element, it’s also a lot more dangerous at the same time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the tech giant of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.

Industry observers note that the proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities.

"Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.

While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the firm's stock price in October.

Recent findings suggest that intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the firm's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an revision to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026.

According to recent reports, A similar upgrade could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010.

Intel's shareholders also allege that the organization had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the company's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the manufacturer's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants.

Charging on Android isn't complicated. Yet, it's more than simply plugging your charger into your phone.

I've learned that an expensive charger is no better than a budget one if it doesn't support your phone's fast-charging protocol. Surely, there are nuances, like heat and battery protection.

But you can rule out most slowdowns when you know your cable's power rating.

Sources indicate that A MacBook app has been my saving grace in sorting out the USB-C cables I charge my Android phones with. Here's how I tested them.

There's much to praise in a USB-C-centric PC like Apple's product. The brand was among the first to go all-in on the port, with the 12-inch MacBook's single USB-C port in 2015. Now, most laptops on the market use it.

The design made my recent cable test easier to run, because I could plug both ends of each cable into my computer's two USB-C ports and read it without any extra hardware.

In a recent development, under the USB-C standard, a cable needs an electronic marker (e-marker) to carry more than 60W or to support USB 3 data. Cables without one, like most USB 2.0 charging cables, are capped at 60W.

I charge my Google Pixel 8 with a 65W Yesido charger and a 240W cable, though the phone draws at most 27W. I believed both were original, but I still wanted proof that the cable lived up to its 240W label.

So I tested it alongside two other cables with WhatCable. The PC software is available for free on its official website and GitHub page, but not on the Mac App Store.

Sources indicate that the download is a 21.5MB zip file that expands to 82.2MB after you unzip it. Because it comes from outside the App Store, your Mac may refuse to open it the first time and warn you that it's from an unidentified developer.

Sources indicate that go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down to the Security section, and click Open Anyway next to the WhatCable message. Then enter your password to confirm.

According to recent reports, the app then opens as a small cable icon in the menu bar in the upper-right corner of the screen. I clicked it, and a panel listed each USB-C port on my Mac as Port-USB-C@1 and Port-USB-C@2.

You'll see a summary of any connection and a cable's e-marker data on WhatCable. A Show technical details toggle in the lower-left corner adds connection data and raw system properties.

A settings menu covers launch at login, empty-port visibility, font size, the menu bar icon, and charging watts in the menu bar.

Much of the app is inaccessible unless you pay for the Pro license, which offers live power graphs, negotiation diagnostics, display diagnostics, cable pin maps, and MagSafe pin diagrams.

Recent findings suggest that the Pro license costs $13 as a one-time purchase for two Macs, which seems fair, although I'm hesitant to throw money at most offers. With the app's basic version, you're good to go.

Of the cables I tested, two are originals: the 1-meter USB-C cable that came with my Meta Quest 3S headset and the 2-in-1 USB-C cable that came with my Maono PD200W mic.

The third is a 240W USB-C cable I share with my phones and PC. For my first test, I plugged both ends of each cable into my PC.

That way, one port supplies power and the other receives it, so the computer can read the cable's e-marker without another device attached.

macOS asked me to allow the accessory to connect, and I clicked Allow. The 240W cable's e-marker reported a rating of 50V at 5A, or 240W, which matches its label.

It's a passive cable, and its data speed is USB 2.0, or 480Mbps. The software noted that the e-marker doesn't report a vendor ID, which is common even on authentic cables.

Many cable makers skip the paid registration with the USB Implementers Forum and leave the field blank, even when the cable performs as rated.

So, a blank vendor ID states more about the maker cutting registration costs than about the cable's quality. That aside, WhatCable couldn't read an e-marker for my USB 2.0 Quest 3S and Maono cables, which was expected.

Recent findings suggest that they don't meet either condition that requires one under the USB-C standard. Also, they were undocumented because Meta and Maono didn't publish ratings for them.

Industry observers note that for my second test, I connected my Pixel 8 to the MacBook with the 240W cable. WhatCable identified the phone and demonstrated a USB Power Delivery (PD) 3.0 connection, which is a protocol that covers charging only.

However, data moves at the speed of the slowest part of the chain, and the 240W cable can only carry USB 2.0 data. So my data connection ran at USB 2.0 speed, even though both devices could go faster.

These results are largely consistent with a previous test I ran, which confirmed that my Pixel 8 charges at its full 27W on this cable, picking 9V at 3A from my Yesido charger.

What I didn't know until now was that it was the wrong cable for moving files to my computer. USB 2.0 maxes out at 480Mbps, which is about 30 to 40MB per second.

A batch of 100 photos should take under 20 seconds, but backing up my 12GB photo folder will take several minutes.

Recent findings suggest that for my third test, I charged my MacBook with the Yesido charger and the 240W cable. WhatCable listed the charger's power options, from 5V at 3A (15W) up to 20V at 3.25A (65W).

According to recent reports, the MacBook took the top option, 20V at 3.25A, for the full 65W. For my fourth test, I swapped in my Maono cable. The charger's top option dropped to 20V at 3A, and the MacBook charged at 60W, costing my MacBook 5W.

However, WhatCable still labeled the connection "Charging well." I only spotted the drop by comparing the two results.

According to recent reports, the Maono cable works with my MacBook, but it isn't fully compatible with my charger's top power option. It's a clear case of a cable limiting the charge, and it gives a strong reason to use the software to catch mismatches.

All my cables look similar in a drawer. But apps like WhatCable offer deeper visibility into my charging system beyond battery capacity and wattage.

In a recent development, they help me rule out the weak links before I trust them with my devices. Incompatible cables aren't necessarily dangerous. Slower charging produces less heat, which is gentler on batteries.

But you'll face bottlenecks if fast charging and transfer are the priority.

InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility.

Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.

Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.

It has been revealed that application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals rapidly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.

Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.

December 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.

It has been revealed that the model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.

In a recent development, some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it swiftly is part of the architecture.

Industry observers note that A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.

In a recent development, the recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.

This is especially vital in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.

The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.

Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author).

The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.

Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author).

According to recent reports, in the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.

According to recent reports, A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.

In a recent development, this distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.

It has been revealed that the reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.

According to recent reports, MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.

The "one place" property is important. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.

Figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author).

The pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.

The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.

Table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view.

It has been revealed that the reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.

According to recent reports, the Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.

Industry observers note that the Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.

Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author).

All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.

The quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.

In practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.

Recent findings suggest that A common event contract is just as important as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.

Industry observers note that the simplified example below reveals a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.

Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.

It has been revealed that the ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.

Recent findings suggest that retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.

Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.

When an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.

The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.

Industry observers note that prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.

The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.

The key design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.

False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.

It has been revealed that human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.

The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.

Recent findings suggest that table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements.

This is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.

In a recent development, the policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.

Figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author).

Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.

The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.

It has been revealed that typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.

Content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.

In a recent development, for regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.

Teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.

Sources indicate that teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.

Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.

The compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.

For customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".

Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.

In regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.

Industry observers note that we expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.

In a recent development, table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements.

Agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:.

The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.
