#511. Are Carbide Chainsaw Chains Worth Paying Extra For?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (506 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Are Carbide Chainsaw Chains Worth Paying Extra For?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whether you regularly use a chainsaw on the job or at home, you may eventually need to replace the chain.
  • Carbide chains have cutting teeth with tips made from tungsten carbide, a compound of tungsten and carbon.
  • However, if you're only occasionally using a chainsaw on your property, a standard model could be the right choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether you regularly use a chainsaw on the job or at home, you may eventually need to replace the chain. This could be a fairly inexpensive purchase, depending on what you buy, as some standard models can range from under $20 up to $30 or more. Carbide chainsaw chains can start under $20 as well, but can go into the hundreds, or even thousands for bulk reels, depending on the model.

Carbide chains have cutting teeth with tips made from tungsten carbide, a compound of tungsten and carbon. By combining with carbon, the tungsten becomes nearly as hard as a diamond, and the compound's melting point is a whopping 5,198 degrees Fahrenheit. Along with the ability to stay sharper longer, carbide chains are an ideal option for cutting tree roots, hardwood, and dirty wood. So if you're tackling demanding tasks and need a durable solution that can handle the pressure, a carbide chain may be the right one for you.

However, if you're only occasionally using a chainsaw on your property, a standard model could be the right choice. Made from hardened steel, a conventional chain can handle everyday tasks like cutting clean firewood. These chains can keep an edge relatively well, and though they might need more sharpening as part of their regular maintenance than a carbide model, standard chains are still a good option. In the end, it's about deciding if what you need the chain for is worth the money you'll spend to get it.

It has been revealed that carbide chainsaw chains can be tougher to sharpen than standard steel chains. In fact, conventional sharpening methods that work on steel chains may not work on carbide. The process is so involved that it might make more sense to just send the chain to a sharpening service to ensure it's done right. That's because carbide chains need specific sharpening equipment, which some pros may not even have.

It has been revealed that improper sharpening can have an impact, especially if one side of the chain is sharper than the other. This could result in the chainsaw pulling to one side as you're cutting, which reduces the amount of control you have over the tool. A dull chain, whether it's carbide or steel, also may not move through the material as effectively as it otherwise would. This means that instead of the chain sliding smoothly through the wood, you may have to physically push down harder than usual. You also may not get wood chips when crosscutting, as a dull chain could instead give you sawdust.

It has been revealed that carbide chains may also not cut through clean wood as fast as a standard steel chain can. This might not be a dealbreaker to some consumers, however, since carbide chains typically keep a sharper edge when working in tougher environments. But if you are mostly cutting clean wood and need to maintain a faster pace, you could potentially notice a difference using a carbide chain.

#508. Breaking: 'Sometimes we are simply scene setting, other times we are helping shape the emotional moments, or enforcing the action' — 007 First Light composers explain how they scored the game to serve both the narrative and the player

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Breaking: 'Sometimes we are simply scene setting, other times we are helping shape the emotional moments, or enforcing the action' — 007 First Light composers explain how they scored the game to serve both the narrative and the player

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, the composers for 007 First Light's soundtrack, joined the project very early by industry standards and could write the score based on advanced footage.
  • Sources indicate that "If I remember correctly, we came on board about 18 months before release," Smith said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming.
  • Smith revealed that with First Light, IO Interactive had a "vertical slice" of the game "already at an advanced level, so he and Henson "could see what the vision for the project really was.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, the composers for 007 First Light's soundtrack, joined the project very early by industry standards and could write the score based on advanced footage.

Sources indicate that "If I remember correctly, we came on board about 18 months before release," Smith said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming. "In the film and TV world, that would be very early, but with games that’s relatively late on.".

Smith revealed that with First Light, IO Interactive had a "vertical slice" of the game "already at an advanced level, so he and Henson "could see what the vision for the project really was.".

Sources indicate that "We still had enough time to feel fully integrated into the audio team at IO Interactive, and to be able to influence gameplay from a music point of view," Henson added. "They are a very welcoming group of people, very open to new ideas and suggestions, and we feel we have made some firm friends.".

The composers explained that for a score like 007 First Light, their primary goal was to give the Bond franchise "a gentle nudge into the modern day, without completely reinventing it," and the cinematic nature of the game allowed them to compose a score that not only served the narrative, but the player.

"There are a lot of 'cinematic' style sections in this game where the music can work more like a traditional non-interactive score, but there are also a lot of parts where the music must guide and inform the player," Smith remarked.

Henson explained that video game projects are always a "mixture" of composing for the game and for the player who can enjoy the game through the music, and it's "one of the reasons we love working on them.".

"Sometimes we are simply scene setting, other times we are helping shape the emotional moments, or enforcing the action," he continued.

"Although for most of the time we hope the player barely notices we are there, the worst thing for an interactive sequence is for the music to jar in some way, to be too intrusive, destroying the immersion and pulling the player out of the game.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

When shopping for a latest lawn mower, some people's first instinct is to shop based on a specific brand. But by only looking at the lawn mower brand itself, you miss an vital part of the equation: the engine. As it turns out, many different lawn mower brands share the same lawn mower engine manufacturer. Take Briggs & Stratton engines, for example. This one engine brand is shared by a variety of different lawn mower brands, including (but not limited to) Toro, Craftsman, Yard Force, Senix, and Troy-Bilt.

With that in mind, your choice of lawn mower may need to go beyond just comparing brand names, deck widths, drive systems, or price tags. If you have a lawn to mow, you should also look for a piece of equipment with a power source you can depend on. Let's look at five of the most popular mower brands that use Briggs & Stratton engines, plus where you can find them.

Toro has one of the more extensive selections of Briggs & Stratton-powered mowers among the five brands listed here. Looking at Lowe's inventory, you'll find a mix of conventional push mowers, self-propelled Recycler models, and the considerably wider TimeMaster, all with Briggs & Stratton engines affixed.

Throughout the Toro catalog, Briggs & Stratton engine displacement ranges from 140 cc to 223 cc. A highlight from the Recycler family in particular is a 21-inch gas self-propelled Recycler with a 140 cc Briggs & Stratton engine. It's priced at $419 and has a customer rating of 4.1 out of 5 stars based on more than 5,200 reviews on Lowe's site. The mower has a bagging attachment included and is recommended for yards measuring between one-quarter and one-half acre.

#502. Who Makes NASA's Rockets, And Where Are They Built?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Who Makes NASA's Rockets, And Where Are They Built?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most of the history of humanity's operations in space, government agencies have taken on the brunt of operations.
  • For example, several hardware components of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), one of the most powerful rockets ever made that is scheduled to take people to the moon as part of the Artemis program, were built by Northrop Grumman in Utah before being transported to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
  • Once completed, it's then transported to Kennedy Space Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For most of the history of humanity's operations in space, government agencies have taken on the brunt of operations. However, NASA gets help from outside manufacturers to build its rockets, working with partners such as Lockheed Martin, L3Harris, Boeing, and Airbus Defense.

For example, several hardware components of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), one of the most powerful rockets ever made that is scheduled to take people to the moon as part of the Artemis program, were built by Northrop Grumman in Utah before being transported to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Meanwhile, NASA's Michoud Facility in New Orleans — which has operated as "America's Rocket Factory" for over 50 years and seen its work introduced from NASA sites in Florida and California — produces the main core stage, which was designed and led by The Boeing Tech giant.

Once completed, it's then transported to Kennedy Space Center. After all of the components arrive at their destination in Florida, they're assembled vertically in NASA's humongous Vehicle Assembly Building. When everything is put together, it's ready for the launchpad.

While you might think it would be best to produce everything needed at Kennedy Space Center, that's not how NASA functions. NASA operates 10 field centers, with Kennedy Space Center being its premier multi-user spaceport. It works with around 100 private-sector partners at the site, employing nearly 250 partnership agreements.

NASA's Booster Fabrication Facility near the spaceport's Launch Complex 39 at the Kennedy Space Center is where the aft skirt and forward assembly for the twin solid rocket boosters used in the SLS are manufactured, assembled, and refurbished. It's primarily operated by Northrop Grumman alongside NASA personnel. The site also upgrades boosters, and has worked on various systems dating back to the Space Shuttle Program.

In a recent development, outside of the rockets and engines needed to send humanity back to the moon, the Artemis program features the Orion spacecraft, which will take astronauts to lunar orbit and return them to Earth. Various components are produced in a variety of locations by several firms. Lockheed Martin performs the primary welding for the Crew Module at the Michoud Assembly Facility, while Airbus Defense and Space produces the European Service Module at its facility in Bremen, Germany. The design work was conducted by Lockheed out of Littleton, Colorado, while various parts and subsystems were produced in California, Upcoming Jersey, and Washington State.

#501. Industry News: A major breakthrough has claimed to set a world record for encoding data onto a quantum computer — and, crucially, reading it back again

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Techradar

Industry News: A major breakthrough has claimed to set a world record for encoding data onto a quantum computer — and, crucially, reading it back again

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moth Quantum says its Tessa technique has achieved a new quantum computing record by storing information on a processor and successfully retrieving it.
  • The method placed 1,568 numerical values across IBM’s 120-qubit Phoenix processor, then used the recovered information to recreate an image.
  • This addresses a major challenge in quantum computing: getting ordinary information into quantum machines and retrieving it without significant loss of accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moth Quantum says its Tessa technique has achieved a new quantum computing record by storing information on a processor and successfully retrieving it.

The method placed 1,568 numerical values across IBM’s 120-qubit Phoenix processor, then used the recovered information to recreate an image.

This addresses a major challenge in quantum computing: getting ordinary information into quantum machines and retrieving it without significant loss of accuracy.

Previous research of this kind recovered 128 numerical values using 12 trapped-ion qubits, making the latest result substantially larger by the study’s definition.

Tessa uses neighboring qubits to control where information is stored, allowing the processor’s existing connections to handle the operation without moving information between distant qubits.

The arrangement avoids extra qubit-moving operations and additional helper qubits, while the tested circuits reached a depth of 19 two-qubit operations.

“Every quantum computer has to get data in before it can do anything useful with it, and that step has been a bottleneck for fields like quantum machine learning,” mentioned Daniel Bultrini, the Moth researcher who developed Tessa.

“Tessa makes the most of the chip’s capabilities, so the whole processor can be put to work at once.”.

Image tests stored 784 and 441 values, requiring 728 and 428 controlled operations, respectively; each used 8,192 measurement attempts.

However, information recovery was imperfect: the largest color image achieved a correlation of 0.69 with its source, compared with 0.95–0.96 for simpler images.

The average numerical error was 0.130 on Phoenix and 0.131 on IBM’s Fez processor, falling to 0.075 and 0.078 after adjustment.

That adjustment used two statistics taken from the original image, meaning the improved reconstruction relied partly on information already known.

For a separate test combining image brightness and color, Phoenix recorded errors of 0.152 and 0.092, while Fez recorded 0.144 and 0.084.

The Phoenix brightness error was 2.6 times higher than the organization’s noise model predicted, indicating that real hardware introduced additional inaccuracies.

Moth Quantum also tried audio, musical notes, DNA, and protein sequences, using different ways to represent information inside the processor.

A music test containing 347 flute notes recovered 18.7% of pitches correctly before adjustment, improving to 49.3% afterward on the Fez processor.

Biological tests required 32,768 measurement attempts, compared with 8,192 for image experiments, yet accuracy varied substantially between sequences for every measurement basis.

The p53 protein sequence achieved 71.5% correct recovery, while Sonic hedgehog reached 76.2% and mitochondrial protein MT-CO3 recorded 92.3% on IBM’s Phoenix hardware.

Results were weaker for other samples: SUR1 reached 22.6%, while pikachurin achieved 25.8%, showing that longer or more complex sequences remained difficult.

The tests also included a mitochondrial DNA sequence containing 784 building blocks and a POLG2 messenger RNA sequence with 1,582.

The study warns that one incorrect DNA or protein unit can matter biologically, so these recovery percentages do not establish dependable medical applications.

The simulations here do not include all interference between neighboring processor groups, and the hardware experiments used no error-correction techniques.

Tessa also depends on a particular pattern of connections between qubits, while measurement demands rise sharply as those connections become more numerous.

Moth Quantum did not use error mitigation, which the study states could reduce reconstruction errors significantly in future hardware tests.

“The quantum applications that will have the greatest impact, including those that work closely with AI, will depend on breakthroughs such as Tessa in order to meet the expectations that have been set,” stated Harry Kumar, Moth’s Founder and CCO.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that finally gave your trusty saw a fresh chain?
  • Your first order of business should be to get out your bar and chain oil and pour an amount that will cover the entire chain in a single container.
  • Quick pop quiz: What happens to metal once it gets warm?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that finally gave your trusty saw a fresh chain? The good news is that this set of teeth will make the saw nearly as good as new. The not-so-good news is that you can't just slap it on, tension it, and go chopping some trees, as you need to do some preventative care first. Generally speaking, maintaining your chainsaw chain proactively can keep rust away. The same applies to one fresh out of the box, but does that include oiling too?

In a recent development, yes. Your first order of business should be to get out your bar and chain oil and pour an amount that will cover the entire chain in a single container. Let the chain soak for a few hours, which will see to it that all the pivot points on the chain are evenly lubricated. After a generous amount of time has passed, take out the chain and hang it up, allowing the excess oil to drip off before putting it on the bar. To help avoid an oily mess, consider hanging the chain above the oil container until the droplets stop, and then install the latest chain.

Quick pop quiz: What happens to metal once it gets warm? It expands. A chainsaw chain has a bunch of pivot points, so the first time you fire up the chainsaw, even if you tension the chain correctly, the heat generated will make it slack again. Thus, you'll need to break in the new chain first. Fortunately, that's relatively easy, albeit a little annoying.

Tension the chain once and then run the tool until it's warm enough. Power off the chainsaw, allow the chain to cool, and readjust the tension to eliminate the slack. Underwhelming as it may be, the new chain still won't be ready for heavier work, which is why it's best to then use the chainsaw for about half an hour just cutting smaller branches. Once the saw finally starts working the way you remember, the whole world (or at least a tree or two) will be your oyster, and you can cut to your heart's content.

In the future, try to incorporate chainsaw maintenance tips and tricks into your routine. Everything matters with this tool. Despite the chain being relatively cheap to purchase, the costs will add up quickly if you start ignoring regular TLC, and you'll burn through chains as if they owe you money. So, clean your tools before and after use, store them correctly, lubricate them frequently, and they will work more reliably and cost less to own.

#497. Industry News: What Exactly Is Stiction & What Causes It?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (424 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Industry News: What Exactly Is Stiction & What Causes It?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that diesel engines are built for tough jobs, from pulling heavy loads to being ideal for long-haul trucking.
  • This means it isn't technically exclusive to diesel engines, although it's used to describe when a moving part inside the diesel engine gets stuck or moves sluggishly instead of sliding back and forth like it's supposed to.
  • Specifically, when engine oil gets too hot, it breaks down and forms a sticky varnish that clings to metal components, which makes diesel engine parts work less efficiently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that diesel engines are built for tough jobs, from pulling heavy loads to being ideal for long-haul trucking. And like any engine, diesels have their pros and cons, one particular issue being stiction. In case the term is unfamiliar, stiction is short for static friction, and it refers to the resistance that must be overcome to get two touching surfaces moving.

This means it isn't technically exclusive to diesel engines, although it's used to describe when a moving part inside the diesel engine gets stuck or moves sluggishly instead of sliding back and forth like it's supposed to. This usually occurs when dirty, degraded oil turns into gunk, preventing engine parts inside from sliding freely.

Specifically, when engine oil gets too hot, it breaks down and forms a sticky varnish that clings to metal components, which makes diesel engine parts work less efficiently. Stiction is often an issue for any engine using HEUI (hydraulically actuated, electronically controlled unit injector) injectors, as they rely on hot, high-pressure engine oil to push fuel into the cylinders. However, stiction is also present in common rail direct fuel injectors, as the engine oil can still break down over time, forming sludge.

According to recent reports, A few different things can cause stiction in diesel engines. For starters, oil degradation is likely the most prominent cause, as extreme heat weakens engine oil over time. When that happens, the oil leaves behind a sticky residue that coats internal parts, preventing the engine from operating smoothly. Not surprisingly, skipped oil changes and poor maintenance are another reason, since the longer you go between changes, the more time oil has to break down. Moisture can be an problem as well, because if the oil never fully warms up, moisture will get in. Frequent short drives can cause this issue to pop up since the engine won't have time to warm up completely.

Cold weather makes the stiction matter even worse because cold oil thickens up. That stated, if the fuel injectors are affected, common signs of stiction include loss of acceleration and overall pulling power, and a shaky idle or an unevenly running engine. Decreased overall fuel efficiency is another symptom. Luckily, there are ways to combat stiction, from using diesel additives to picking a high-grade synthetic diesel oil. The latter can help keep the injectors clean and give the engine the strongest defense against wear. Additionally, sticking to a regular oil change schedule and using a quality oil filter will go a long way too.

#495. Breaking: How Do They Build Underwater Tunnels?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (854 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Breaking: How Do They Build Underwater Tunnels?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tunnels are easy for groundhogs to dig; not so much for humans, even with our persistence.
  • It has been revealed that the Thames Tunnel in London began construction in 1825, took 18 years to build, and was the third such attempt at such an under-river crossing.
  • Industry observers note that there were a few advancements that improved the tunnel shield during the 1800s: the conversion from a square shield to a circular one; the introduction of compressed air helped keep water away from the dig, and; the injection of a grout lining to reduce impacts from settlement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tunnels are easy for groundhogs to dig; not so much for humans, even with our persistence. That is especially true when those tunnels are underwater, yet somehow, many of us have daily commutes that take us from one side of a harbor to the other. You might know of those giant tunnel boring machines or TBMs that have made the job of cutting earth easier and safer — Virginia's largest-ever infrastructure project underneath the Chesapeake River was recently helped along by a TBM named Mary — but the origin of underwater tunneling might be a bit more boring (pun intended) than you'd think.

It has been revealed that the Thames Tunnel in London began construction in 1825, took 18 years to build, and was the third such attempt at such an under-river crossing. British-French engineer Marc Brunel patented a tunnel shield that he said was inspired by how a naval shipworm ate through wood: boards lined a cap between the dirt and miners who would open each one of them, dig out several inches behind, close the board, and repeat. Once a full section was cleared, workers would auger the shield forward while bricklayers furnished the actual tunnel. At about a quarter of a mile long, the job caused the occasional flood, claimed six workers' lives and the good health of many others. Unlike those earlier attempts, however, this project didn't get washed out. The tunnel opened to pedestrian traffic in 1843.

Industry observers note that there were a few advancements that improved the tunnel shield during the 1800s: the conversion from a square shield to a circular one; the introduction of compressed air helped keep water away from the dig, and; the injection of a grout lining to reduce impacts from settlement. Wood and brick gave way to cement and steel. But it would take more than a century before tunnel cutters came into their own.

In the space between came another technique that was first recorded in the 1890s called immersed tube construction. For modern projects, sections of tunnel are fabricated above ground and then literally floated on-site by tug boats before a catamaran cradling barge aligns it into position. Ballast is loaded onto the tube portion to gently lower them onto a dredged and filled bed. The barge finally drags the tunnel section into its awaiting stub. The interlocking between the two sections is drained and fill material is then dumped to cover the connection. The first transportation tunnel to be built with this general method was the Michigan Central Railway Tunnel in 1906 which connected Detroit with its Canadian neighbor of Windsor, Ontario, just over a mile away.

Not every subaqueous crossing calls for boring machines or pre-cast tubes. For its Big Dig, the city of Boston partially drained the once-busy Fort Point shipping channel to construct an approach tube to a larger harbor crossing in the mid 1990s. A mix of somewhat novel techniques were used to keep the soil from collapsing in on the site while protecting the nearby Gilette razor manufacturing facility as well as existing subway tunnels. Engineers injected columns of grout to stabilize the ground before later refrigerating a grid of brine-filled pipes to freeze another section. This allowed MBTA Red Line trains to continue running just five feet below where a upcoming underwater highway ramp was to be. Other tunnels in the Big Dig project, including that harbor crossing, also used immersed tube construction and other MBTA services including the commuter rail were not impacted during more than two decades of work.

In a recent development, attempts at cutting machines in the 19th century were unsuccessful. Belgian engineer Henri-Joseph Maus built a so-called "Mountain Slicer" in 1846 to tunnel through the Alps, but subsequent populist revolutions cut off his Sardinian royal line of credit. At the foot of the Hoosac Range of Massachusetts, the Wilson Patented Stone-Cutting Machine made it through about 10 feet of rock before giving up the goat in 1851.

Fast forward to 1952 when mining engineer James Robbins developed the first successful tunnel-boring machine that was put to use building Oahe Dam in South Dakota. Ahead of the machine's worker shield was a rotating head filled with incisors and cutting discs that worked at the site's soft shale rock. Designs have changed over time as further projects presented grander requirements, tighter constraints, and upcoming embedded challenges. For example, in soft soil conditions, a slurry shield may be used where liquidized clay is pumped into the cutter head to maintain pressurized conditions favorable for excavating the soil. This mixed sludge is pumped back through the shield, and the clay is then separated for re-use.

Sources indicate that TBMs are used for all sorts of tunnels, including those running underwater. 19 machines were used over the course of a dozen years to build Sydney Metro's network of transit tubes, a good portion of which run underneath harbors, rivers, and bays. Meanwhile, The Boring Company, an Elon Musk venture wants to use a TBM to create a 200-mph tunnel between San Antonio and Austin, Texas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norwegian maritime engineering tech giant Kongsberg Maritime wants to convert commercial fishing trawlers into autonomous vessels capable of hunting Russian submarines for Britain's Royal Navy.

Its Arctic Hunter concept uses an existing 56-meter fishing vessel design, approximately 184 feet long, modified to conduct underwater surveillance without carrying a crew.

The proposed conversion would replace fishing equipment with autonomous navigation systems, submarine detection sonar, and secure communications equipment for extended maritime operations.

Kongsberg states each vessel would carry sonar equipment supplied by Thales UK alongside protected communications technology.

The ships are expected to operate independently for approximately 60 days, allowing them to undertake extended assignments without requiring onboard personnel.

Kongsberg also intends to modify certain components, including the propulsion system, to minimize unwanted underwater noise that might interfere with acoustic monitoring equipment.

The proposed design falls under Britain's Type 92 program, which seeks relatively affordable autonomous vessels capable of assisting conventional warships with anti-submarine warfare assignments.

The concept draws inspiration from World War II, when Britain converted commercial whaling vessels into naval escorts to protect shipping against German submarines.

Kongsberg Maritime argues that commercial shipbuilding already offers suitable vessel designs for demanding North Atlantic conditions, reducing the need for completely latest military construction.

The organization describes its approach as a maritime engineering exercise rather than conventional weapons development.

Kongsberg's proposed deployment arrangement involves 10 autonomous vessels operating from a support location west of the Bear Gap, between Norway and Svalbard.

That maritime passage connects northern waters with the Atlantic, making it an crucial geographical reference in discussions about Russian submarine movements.

Establishing the vessels' support facilities closer to their intended operating area would reduce the distance they must travel before beginning assignments.

But Kongsberg Maritime indicates it would manufacture the proposed Type 92 vessels within Britain if selected to deliver the program.

The Arctic Hunter ships would operate alongside Britain's future Type 26 frigates, which BAE Systems is constructing for several allied naval forces.

Those warships are intended for the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and Norway, with autonomous vessels potentially providing additional surveillance support.

The arrangement fits Britain's aims for a hybrid naval fleet combining conventional warships with remotely operated or independently navigating surface vessels.

However, Kongsberg has only outlined its proposed design, and there is no official confirmation that Britain has awarded it a construction contract.

Tech Report: Should You Buy A 2-Stroke Or 4-Stroke Outboard Motor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, outboards come in different designs and sizes, and picking the right one can make a tangible difference in how a boat runs.
  • For starters, the biggest difference is how each engine burns fuel to create power.
  • It has been revealed that because of their less complex build with fewer internal parts, 2-stroke outboard motors can put out a lot of power without being as heavy as a similar 4-stroke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, outboards come in different designs and sizes, and picking the right one can make a tangible difference in how a boat runs. So, it's no surprise that boat owners have spent a long time debating between 2-stroke and 4-stroke engines (vocal opinions come with the territory of boat ownership). Both of these outboard motors have disadvantages, but with current technology, those drawbacks are on a much smaller scale than they were in the past. As such, which one to buy will likely depend on personal choice and the boat type.

For starters, the biggest difference is how each engine burns fuel to create power. A 2-stroke motor completes its full power cycle in just two up-and-down movements of the piston, firing every time the crankshaft makes a full turn. On the other hand, a 4-stroke motor needs four piston movements and two full turns of the crankshaft to complete that same single power cycle.

It has been revealed that because of their less complex build with fewer internal parts, 2-stroke outboard motors can put out a lot of power without being as heavy as a similar 4-stroke. In fact, compared to its 4-stroke cousin with the same horsepower, a 2-stroke outboard motor tends to produce more power. Its smaller size also makes it a great fit for smaller boats.

Having stated that, you might think the choice is obvious. Yet, modern 4-stroke motors generally burn less fuel than 2-stroke models, especially during recreational use. Additionally, 4-stroke outboard motors have reduced emissions and are quieter. That's not to say they aren't capable of producing great power, considering that one of the most powerful outboard boat engines ever built is a 4-stroke.

When it comes to the not-so-great things about these motors, the most noticeable disadvantage of a 4-stroke outboard motor is the size. While technology has made them lighter and more compact compared to older models, 4-stroke motors can still be too bulky for smaller boats. Also, due to their more elaborate design, they typically require more maintenance. A good example is Yamaha outboard motors, for which the tech giant lists extra items needed for the maintenance of 4-stroke models. Having additional components also means there are more parts that could potentially need fixing down the road/waterway. "Potentially" is the key word here because these motors are generally known for their dependability.

According to recent reports, as for 2-stroke outboard motors, they're usually categorized as noisier and less fuel-efficient. Older models (especially those with carburetors) have a reputation for rough idling and compromised stability at lower RPMs. In addition, their lubrication system isn't as good at shielding internal parts from wear and tear. Nevertheless, a lot of the above is based on older models, as contemporary 2-strokes have fewer issues with fuel efficiency, for example.

It has been revealed that ultimately, due to technological advancements, 2-strokes and 4-strokes are considerably more comparable than before. The 4-stroke outboard engines are more common in the market these days, though the choice of which one to buy still comes down to preference. It's best to research individual motors first if a specific one tickles your fancy.

It will examine trust, response quality, comprehension and everyday health actions when people use conversational health AI.

The research experience is Apple’s design, built on AI technology from OpenEvidence. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, with the right funds and the right parts, it's possible to build a computer that rivals some of the more recent consoles. That includes the Nintendo Switch 2. But how much would the total cost actually be, and what would you need to make it happen? With some intuitive shopping, this modern PC build would cost anywhere between $800 and $1,000. You can trim costs in some areas, but ultimately, that's what you're looking at to build a machine capable of matching the Nintendo Switch 2 from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that before you can dive into any of that, you need to know the Switch 2's internal hardware specifications. According to PCSpecs.io, the Nintendo Switch 2 has an ARM Cortex-A78C 8-core, 8-thread processor, capable of 1.1 GHz clock speeds. It also runs on a custom Nvidia Ampere GPU with 12 GB of LPDDR5 system RAM, with about 9 GB of that memory allocated to games. Altogether, it's capable of 3.07 teraflops of performance and has a memory bandwidth of 102 GB/s in docked mode. For the GPU alone, that's the equivalent of an Nvidia RTX 3050. However, the Switch 2's GPU has fewer CUDA cores, making it less powerful than the desktop graphics card.

Here's where things get a bit hairy. Given that prices can rapidly fluctuate, keep in mind that the total cost can change by the time you're reading this. Right now, you can buy an Nvidia RTX 3050 for between $250 and $300. 16 GB of DDR5 RAM can cost between $240 and $400, though you can get by with half of that or downgrade to something like the Crucial 16GB DDR4 RAM Kit for around $135. With a 4-core, 8-thread processor and a base clock speed of 3.3 GHz, the Intel Core i3-12100F is a comparable CPU that costs around $150. So, for the GPU, CPU, and RAM, you're looking at a base price of at least $640, or $535 if you choose DDR4 RAM.

You'll also need a motherboard, hard drive or solid-state drive, a PC case, power supply, and accessories, whether that's a controller or a mouse and keyboard set. Plus, you'll want speakers and, if you initiative to play online, you'll want a microphone or headset. The motherboard, case, and power supply will add between $50 and $100 for each item. With the hard drive shortage, you're looking at another $100 to $350 for a decent-sized storage drive. Adding all of that together, not including some of the other extras, you're in the $800 to $1,000 range. Granted, these are rough estimates, but that's still quite a bit higher than the Switch 2's current $500 price tag.

It has been revealed that at the risk of sounding like an aging tech enthusiast, there was a time when building a PC like this would have cost much less. We are no longer at that point, nor will we be for quite some time, if ever again. RAM shortages and rising PC parts costs are to blame for that. But this also means that the estimated prices listed here will change over time. With some careful planning, and by using retailer promotions and sales, you could build a PC that's equivalent to a Switch 2 for much less. It's no wonder why building a machine to compete with more powerful consoles like the PS5 Pro is prohibitively expensive.

You can make some concessions and go with a less powerful and more accessible GPU, CPU, or RAM bundle — the suggestion to go with the lower-cost DDR4 RAM is precisely that. Not that this is recommended, but you could also opt for renewed or refurbished parts, specifically the GPU. But this also highlights how the Nintendo Switch 2, which costs $500 all-in, could be an enticing buy for many who don't want to bother putting together their own system.

The Nintendo Switch 2 also has a lot of unique features that even most owners don't know about, which improve the gaming experience. The Joy-Con controllers and their versatility are just one example, as is breaking out the console anywhere for some spur-of-the-moment local multiplayer sessions. Though, you can also connect Joy-Cons to a PC for gaming using Steam. You can also grab one of the other handheld consoles to play anywhere, most of which are cheaper or comparable to the cost of building your own system.

It intends to spend the latest capital on additional computing infrastructure and recruitment, particularly for research involving open-source AI models.

Mount Thor aims to establish a laboratory for testing open-source models adapted to Apple processors, potentially reducing costs for certain workloads.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While I've been a Samsung Galaxy user longer than I've been a Google Pixel user, I've always relied on Google Photos on all my Samsung devices.

Not because of the convenience of Google Photos features, but because it's streamlined with my Google One storage.

When Samsung ended its partnership with OneDrive as default cloud storage, it replaced it with Google storage, giving me a solid reason to consider going back to the Samsung Gallery app.

I've tested the Google storage integration, and I realized how invaluable it is, and now it's starting to win me back to Samsung Gallery.

I love how well Samsung Gallery runs on Galaxy devices, as it is snappy and works fantastically even offline.

However, it was always held back by its cloud backup tool: OneDrive.

Rather than tying into Google, it used OneDrive for years, which made it less ideal since most consumers have Google storage linked to their Android account.

In my case, I also had little reason to rely on OneDrive, as I use Google Workspace from Gmail to office tools like Docs and Sheets over Microsoft's suite.

It also forced me to use Google Photos, and although backing up my photos with Google isn't straightforward, it serves as better, more secure storage for my vital memories taken with my Galaxy devices.

Samsung Gallery is an incredible platform, held back only by OneDrive. It's the last remaining thorn that has always pushed me toward Google Photos on my Samsung devices.

But now that OneDrive is out of the picture, I have more reason to ditch Google Photos for Samsung Gallery.

It didn't take long for them to pick Google as the replacement for the Gallery.

Sources indicate that the integration was recently rolled out to supported devices, arriving alongside One UI 9. Even better, the setup is just as seamless as it was with OneDrive.

Plus, Google One offers a larger free tier at 15GB than OneDrive, which typically starts at 5GB and only expands when bundled with other perks.

In the Gallery app, there's a dedicated setting that lets you configure your backup using Google storage.

Open the cloud settings and pick the Google account you want to sync; it indicates all the Google profiles right now logged in to your Samsung device.

That requires minimal effort compared to dealing with Microsoft or creating a separate account just to start syncing with OneDrive.

I also ensured that the same Samsung account was active and logged in on the phone I wanted to use.

When configured, it automatically backs up my photos and videos.

There's a minor quirk after you've set it up: you can't easily switch Google accounts after you finish setup.

It requires turning off sync and removing the account from your Samsung device, and setting it up again.

I wish this could be remedied in the future without the added hurdle when switching Google profiles.

It always makes sense to stick with Google storage on Samsung hardware, and it removes the need to use Google Photos while my media still syncs automatically.

Direct cloud storage makes it easy to skip Google Photos and manage my Samsung photos and videos in the Gallery app.

Another thing I like is cross-device sync, so I can view and access my media on my Galaxy tablet or Galaxy Z Flip, and vice versa.

There's also an easier way to manage which albums and folders are uploaded.

In Settings, I can toggle specific albums on or off and disable sync with one tap.

While I still have Google Photos set up on my Galaxy devices, everything works without hiccups when it comes to duplicates.

These files aren't duplicated, meaning that even if they are backed up in Google Photos and simultaneously set to sync via Samsung Gallery, redundant copies aren't created.

Customers can sync across both gallery apps without friction while saving cloud capacity.

If you're running short on memory, there's also a Free up space feature, though I haven't seen it on my Galaxy Z Flip 7 yet, since Samsung is limiting its availability.

Basically, it works the same way as in Google Photos, letting users remove local photos and videos that are safely saved in the cloud.

It helps free up a solid chunk of space on my Samsung device, a trick I've always found useful in Google Photos.

However, there's the obvious quirk that you need a stable internet connection to access those cloud items after they are deleted locally.

Instead, you get thumbnails and previews saved on your phone with the option to download the files back locally when needed.

It is always nice to have that safety net, especially for people who frequently get low-storage warnings.

You can use the Google Files app to scan for duplicate and junk files and remove them with a few taps.

It always made sense to use Google storage on Samsung devices, which is why I was relieved and happy to see this massive upgrade on the Gallery app.

I'm still waiting for the Free up space tool to arrive on my device so I can test whether cloud previews feel as reliable as locally saved media.

So far, I'm thrilled with the added convenience on my Galaxy phones. It proves Samsung realized forcing a Microsoft cloud storage down Android people' throats would never beat Google integration.

Critics liked the noise cancellation, but it comes with a catch. Critics noticed that audio quality suffers as soon as you turn on ANC, which limits its usability. To keep the price down, Baseus left out wear detection, a bare-minimum feature many headphones offer. One thing that did impress critics about this headset is its amazing battery life. The Inspire XH1 can last 100 hours on a full charge with ANC off. That number drops to 65 hours with noise cancellation, which is still more than enough for most users.

Overall, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless is a decent pair of headphones for $399.99. Reviewers liked the sound — Trusted Reviews praised the tonally rich audio, while What Hi-Fi? was a fan of the refined sound presentation. The midrange also sounded very impressive in their tests. The noise cancellation is where things get tricky. SoundGuys noted decent ANC, but Trusted Reviews noted its struggles in noisy environments.

It's far more minimalist than previous models, with metallic accents adding a premium touch. Critics say the large earcups are comfortable enough for long sessions, though the fact that the device doesn't fold entirely makes it a bit of a pain to carry around. Don't expect an IP rating if you're hoping to go for a swim with the Momentum 5 Wireless wrapped snugly around your head.

Recent findings suggest that most people know Sonos for its stellar home theater music systems. The Sonos Arc Ultra is arguably the best soundbar on the market, and pairing it with a Sub 4 and two Era 300 speakers completes your home theater audio setup. However, their headphones have been playing catch-up to the best major headphone brands for a while. Sources indicate that even people deep in the Sonos ecosystem will find this headset a hard sell, with T3 noting that its integration with other Sonos products isn't great. PCMag appreciated the warm audio response, while What Hi-Fi? found the sound output rich and powerful, especially in the bass. ANC gets the job done for most critics, and they called the sleek, comfortable design the cherry on top. In fact, this improved ANC sealed the deal for us in our review of the Sonos Ace Ultra.

The Nothing Headphone (a) is yet another good option for anyone seeking out a budget-friendly pair of noise-canceling headphones. It's fantastic value for $199, and a cheaper $130.99 price tag at the time of writing makes it an even more tantalizing proposition. At this price, we consider it the best headphones you can buy. Speaking of which, critics largely praised the noise cancellation, though there are some caveats. Sound quality is also mixed, if reviewers are to be believed. It was mostly praised by reviewers, with TechRadar stating that this headset is a notable upgrade over the Headphone (a). However, PCMag wasn't a huge fan of the bass-heavy audio presentation, and SoundGuys wasn't a huge fan of the stock sound tuning. While the design itself may not be to your taste, comfort is one area where the Headphone (a) won't disappoint. Jack Wall, the composer for the original Mass Effect, has shared the story of how he landed the job on BioWare's now-iconic sci-fi role-playing game (RPG).

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Wall recalled that he was offered a chance to audition for Mass Effect after working on Jade Empire and "had a pretty good time doing that.".

"Of course, then it had a code name: 'SFX'," Wall recalled. "It was a mystery.".

The composer explained that he created some demo music, then got a call shortly after from BioWare producer Shauna Perry, who told Wall they did a blind audition of all the entries to single out their favorite.

Sources indicate that "No one knew whose music was attributed to which composer," he stated. "They gravitated to mine and were very happy to find out it was me! I love that story because I had to earn it.".

Sources indicate that wall continued, saying, "I went to BioWare in Edmonton to do our kickoff meeting, and they noted there was this one composer, Sam Hulick, who did this one piece that they really liked (the demo that became 'Uncharted Worlds'). I think I said, 'Why did you hire me?' (laughs).".

'Uncharted Worlds' is, of course, one of Mass Effect's most memorable tracks, and Hulick also came on board, too.

According to recent reports, "He was very young in his career at the time, so they were reluctant to hire him outright on his own, but having us both made sense," Wall said. "I honestly love that piece, and Sam killed it.".

Recent findings suggest that the Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 scores were a collaborative effort, featuring Wall, Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates, with Jimmy Hinson lending his talent on the sequel. They're two of the best RPG soundtracks of all time, and according to Wall, the other BioWare developers had their favorite tracks.

Namely, 'Vigil', 'Uncharted Worlds', 'The Normandy', and 'The Citadel', Wall mentioned, adding that game director Casey Hudson called him after he'd completed 'Noveria' and told him, "This was his dream piece fulfilling the brief he had asked for initially.".

"From ME2, of course, 'Suicide Mission', 'The Illusive Man' and 'Reflections'," Wall added. "I’m going from memory here, so opinions on the dev team may vary!".

Wall also told TechRadar Gaming that 'Suicide Mission' was one of the first things he and Casey Hudson worked on together and is "Probably to date one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever.".

So, can you get the same mulching performance with your regular blades?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that investing in a home solar array became less attractive when the federal tax credit on energy-efficient installations ended in 2025. Even as panel production prices (for all different types of consumer solar panels) have continued to fall, the average quote for even a modest build in the United States can push above $20,000. As the leading state in solar projects, California has been at the brunt of a further decrease in returns as the Net Energy Metering 3.0 scheme in 2023 reduced prices for midday solar generation in the hopes of getting more residential battery projects into gear to supply the evening peak hours.

Industry observers note that A new wave of tariffs coming into effect in December will establish high floor prices on a key solar panel component, potentially pushing the breakeven period of a solar-only installation right up to if not past its typical useful life. As states have migrated their solar-based credit and rebate programs towards battery generation events, you're probably better off going with a solar and battery project for your home than a pure solar one.

According to recent reports, solar marketplace research firm EnergySage currently estimates project breakeven points running between 8 years in a state like California to 24 years in Alabama for an average-size build respective to each state. Many states fall within the 10- to 15-year timeframe, including Illinois, Fresh York, Pennsylvania, and Texas. Keep in mind that these panels have an expected lifespan of anywhere between 20 and 35 years, depending on how new the installation is. These calculations do not include any applicable solar installation incentives, such as they are available from states.

Industry observers note that expect to wait longer for your payback if you're installing after December 4 as a wave of so-called Section 232 tariffs (which have also been used against steel and other metals used in home improvement tools from the likes of DeWalt and Craftsman) issued in August concerning polysilicon, a key component of photovoltaic panels, comes into effect. Imports of finished solar modules will be subject to a minimum sale price of 38 cents per watt plus a value-added tax of up to 15%.

Sources indicate that disregarding the VAT, this represents a 20% to 50% increase from today's prices at common sources. Installers could decide to cut their non-fungible overhead — elements including labor, marketing, and margin that make up nearly half of the bill, according to EnergySage — to pass on a lower increase, at least initially. Still, even a single-digit percentage premium could mean an extra $1,000 or $2,000 to your bill.

In a recent development, many states and utilities now offer installation and generation incentives for residential stored power projects. For example, energy providers in Massachusetts offer up to $1,375 a year for up to 60 summertime activations at 5kW output. In neighboring Rhode Island, the state will rebate builds at $250 per kilowatt-hour ($500 for property owners with eligible incomes) for the first 25kW of capacity and $175/kWh for further capacity on larger plots up to 250kW.

Tesla's Powerwall series of batteries are a go-to choice (though not the only one) for many proprietors and can make sense as part of an integrated setup with a smaller solar array for about the same price as going solar-only. You'll want to evaluate your own usage, brush up on incentive programs available to you, and then match those specs to products on the market to maximize your potential returns. This is all on top of the extra breathing room and peace of mind you get if and when a grid outage occurs — keeping the fridge running means you can tack on a trip's worth of groceries to your overall savings.

#481. Industry News: Do Electric Tankless Water Heaters Work As Well As Gas?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)

Industry News: Do Electric Tankless Water Heaters Work As Well As Gas?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tankless water heaters are, as the name suggests, household appliances that provide hot water on demand without relying on a storage tank.
  • There are two main types of tankless water heaters: gas-powered and electric.
  • According to recent reports, gas tankless water heaters also have the advantage during cooler months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tankless water heaters are, as the name suggests, household appliances that provide hot water on demand without relying on a storage tank. They work by bringing cold water into the device's heat exchanger, where it rapidly increases in temperature and comes out the other end as hot water. Tankless water heaters have a few drawbacks, from higher upfront installation costs to reduced performance in cold temperatures, but are arguably better than conventional tank-style heaters in several ways. Because these devices heat water on demand, owners will technically never run out of hot water. Plus, they're more energy efficient, take up less space, and have a longer lifespan, capable of lasting 20 years with proper maintenance. For the right house, a tankless water heater is a worthwhile upgrade.

There are two main types of tankless water heaters: gas-powered and electric. While both perform well, gas models are generally better. The main reason is that gas tankless water heaters can deliver higher hot-water flow rates than electric models. Flow rate is the amount of water being discharged, measured in gallons per minute (GPM). Depending on the model, a gas-powered unit can deliver 4.5 GPM, plenty to support showers, faucets, and other appliances simultaneously, all without being super taxing on electrical systems.

According to recent reports, gas tankless water heaters also have the advantage during cooler months. Gas heaters have burner capacities ranging from 140,000 to 199,000 Btu/h. By comparison, residential electric heaters have roughly equivalent capacities of 47,770 to 109,100 Btu/h (14 to 32 kW). This means that gas tankless models have a higher heating capacity to raise the temperature of incoming water to the desired level.

Overall costs play a huge role when buying a water heater. Upfront, gas heaters are more expensive. A typical gas model will run you $1,160 on average, and that doesn't account for installation costs. Electric heaters, on the other hand, will cost you an average of $650. That may sound great, but operating costs are higher. Many electric units require a minimum of 120 amps and multiple 240V circuits to run— that's a lot of power. To put that into perspective, a conventional electric tank water heater only needs 18.8 amps at 240V. If your house can't provide enough power, then you'll need to upgrade the electrical panel. And a full panel upgrade can cost up to $2,000.

The environment also plays an notable role, as colder climates are harder on electric heaters. An electrical unit rated at 5GPM might only output 3GPM if it has to heat up cold groundwater and the power demand is high. A high-powered 36 kW unit will need to draw in 150 amps to heat up water by 80 degrees Fahrenheit. That is a ton of energy, and it puts a lot of pressure on a house's electrical infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that back in 2019, Consumer Reports tested gas and electric tankless water heaters. They found that when the incoming water was warm at 74 degrees Fahrenheit, both the gas and electric models were able to heat and maintain the water. However, when the water was 58 degrees Fahrenheit, the electric unit struggled to deliver. It's for this reason that electric heaters are recommended for mild climates where the groundwater is warmer.

In a recent development, despite their shortcomings, there are still some scenarios where an electric tankless water heater is a better option than a gas unit. For example, small living spaces or households that don't utilize a lot of hot water for appliances are perfect. Demand in these locations is low, so an electric heater won't be too taxing on your home's electrical or water systems. Also, these machines work better in warmer climates.

Sources indicate that although gas-powered heaters perform better in colder months, they still perform well during warmer weather. It's just that the gap between gas and electric is much smaller. Warm climates have warmer groundwater, which means that the machines can use less energy to heat water. Electric units are better in this scenario because they are cheaper upfront. Additionally, gas water heaters produce exhaust and need a ventilation system. With electric units, that's not an issue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shipments of x86 CPUs declined quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year in the third quarter as demand for client processors dropped sharply due to high component prices, while server CPU unit sales grew by a whopping 20% year-over-year, according to the latest report from Mercury Research. Intel regained overall CPU market share from AMD for the first time since Q2 2025, largely due to surprisingly strong performance in desktop PCs. Meanwhile, AMD continued to set latest records in the mobile and server CPU segments, the report claims. In total, the industry supplied 68.93 million x86 CPUs, Jon Peddie Research reports.

All CPUs, including IoT and SoCs.

The overall CPU market contracted both sequentially and year-over-year in unit shipments in Q3 2026, after a much stronger-than-expected second quarter, according to Mercury Research. AMD and Intel shipped 60.8 million client CPUs and 8.13 million data center processors during the quarter. One thing to keep in mind about the reports from JPR and Mercury Research is that they count CPU shipments, which happen months before those CPUs are sold in actual systems.

"After a far better than expected second quarter market for client processors, the third quarter PC CPU market declined far more than expected, entirely due to a downturn in mobile CPUs — this was the same segment that was unexpectedly higher last quarter, hinting that part of the downturn may have been due to CPU demand pulling in sales from the third quarter," mentioned Dean McCarron, principal analyst at Mercury Research.

Sources indicate that "Both Intel and AMD indicated in their earnings results that there was a rapid softening in PC demand late in the third quarter that impacted client processor shipments and that the outlook for client CPUs in the fourth quarter will be a decline in excess of 20%. Unlike client CPUs, however, server processors continued to grow strongly in the past quarter, as did embedded CPUs.".

Quarter over quarter, the decline was driven primarily by significantly lower demand for mobile processors, as 86 notebook CPU shipments dropped by more than 10%. By contrast, desktop CPU shipments recovered, largely thanks to Intel, while server and embedded CPU shipments continued to grow strongly. Excluding IoT, semi-custom SoCs, and embedded products, both AMD and Intel shipped fewer x86 processors than in the previous quarter, though AMD's decline was larger than Intel's.

In a recent development, compared with the third quarter of 2025, CPU shipments declined across all major market segments except servers. Desktop and notebook CPU shipments decreased due to weaker PC demand amid rising component costs, particularly memory prices. Embedded processor and semi-custom SoC shipments also declined, primarily due to AMD's shrinking game console business. By contrast, fueled by the ongoing buildout of AI infrastructure, server CPU shipments increased by more than 20% YoY, their highest annual growth rate in nearly five years.

According to recent reports, "Client CPU shipments softened in Q3 as OEMs kept inventories lean and the DIY channel remained weak," noted Dr. Jon Peddie, president of Jon Peddie Research. "Server CPUs continued growing, with AMD gaining share and AI-related demand supporting the market. We expect PC conditions to remain difficult into the first half of 2027.".

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Due to weakness in the client PC space, AMD's overall x86 market share (excluding embedded and semi-custom SoC) declined by 0.6% QoQ for the first time in years, but still grew by a significant 4.5% YoY, according to Mercury Research.

In the x86 client PC segment, Intel regained some ground on AMD in Q3 2026 as overall client CPU shipments declined more sharply than expected, according to both Jon Peddie Research and Mercury Research. JPR estimates that AMD and Intel shipped 60.8 million client processors in Q3 2026, down from 62.93 million a quarter before and roughly 65 million in Q3 2025.

Recent findings suggest that AMD's client CPU unit share dropped to 29.3%, down from a record 30.3% in Q2, but still notably higher than the 25.4% it commanded a year earlier. Meanwhile, Intel increased its share to 70.7%, though its position remained considerably weaker than in Q3 2025, when it controlled 74.6% of the market.

According to recent reports, intel's sequential market share gains were driven entirely by a substantial increase in desktop CPU shipments, while AMD continued to gain ground in notebooks, albeit at a much slower pace than in previous quarters. Mercury Research believes that weaker demand for mobile CPUs may have enabled Intel to allocate more silicon to desktop processors, a market that the tech giant had undersupplied for some time.

However, the outlook for both companies' client CPU businesses is rather gloomy, as rising component costs (especially DRAM and 3D NAND prices) are weighing on PC demand. Both AMD and Intel anticipate a sequential decline in client CPU shipments of more than 20% in the fourth quarter and further declines in the year to come. Meanwhile, one has to keep in mind that CPUs sold in Q4 are meant for systems to be shipped in Q1, which is traditionally weak. Hence, while the 20% YoY decline is extraordinary, a substantial part of that decline is seasonal.

In the desktop PC segment, Intel made a spectacular comeback in Q3 2026, reclaiming 5% of the market in one quarter. Intel's desktop CPU unit share climbed to 70.1%, up 5% sequentially and 3.7% in the same quarter a year ago. By contrast, AMD's share dropped to 29.9%, down from 34.9% in Q2 2026 and 33.6% in Q3 2025, meaning the tech giant wiped out its market share gains over the past year.

Mercury Research speculates that weaker demand for notebook processors enabled Intel to allocate more silicon to mainstream desktop CPUs, a market that both companies have underserved for some time. Another factor behind AMD's poor performance was its greater exposure to the gaming PC market, which suffered from limited availability of gaming graphics cards and unusually high costs for other components, such as memory modules and SSDs.

Yet, desktops became the only major x86 CPU market segment where AMD lost unit share both sequentially and year-over-year.

In the mobile PC segment, both AMD and Intel saw a substantial decline in CPU shipments in Q3 2026 as the market contracted more than 10% sequentially, according to Mercury Research. However, AMD's shipments declined slightly less than Intel's, which enabled the company to increase its mobile CPU unit share to a record 29.2%, up from 28.9% in Q2 2026 and 21.9% in Q3 2025. Intel remained the dominant supplier with a 70.8% share, down from 71.1% in the previous quarter and 78.1% a year earlier.

Although AMD's sequential market share gain of 0.2% was negligible, its 7.2% YoY gain was impressive, especially given Intel's historically strong position in the notebook market. Mercury Research attributes the sharp sequential decline in mobile CPU shipments partly to PC makers pulling forward their CPU procurements into the unusually strong second quarter.

Unfortunately for both AMD and Intel, the outlook for the fourth quarter is gloomy, as rising memory and other component prices drive up notebook prices and reduce end-user demand.

Recent findings suggest that unlike the bleak client CPU market, server CPUs are thriving, with shipments of data center processors reaching 8.13 million units in Q3 2026, according to Jon Peddie Research. The market again grew 20% year-over-year, the highest annual growth rate in nearly five years, according to Mercury Research.

In a recent development, in the server CPU segment, AMD continued its winning spree as its unit share reached a record 35.5%, up from 34.5% in Q2 2026 and 27.8% in Q3 2025. Intel remained the dominant supplier with a 64.5% share, down 1% sequentially and 7.7% year-over-year.

Interestingly, Intel managed to slow AMD's advance in the core data center CPU market by apparently substantially increasing shipments of its Xeon SP processors, McCarron believes. When the comparison is limited to AMD's EPYC and Intel's Xeon SP processors, AMD's unit share reached 46.8%, up just 0.4% sequentially, which represents AMD's smallest sequential gain over the past year, as the manufacturer's quarterly share gains by this metric averaged 3% over the preceding three quarters.

Sources indicate that unlike the client CPU market, the outlook for the server processor market remains particularly favorable for both AMD and Intel. The ongoing buildout of AI infrastructure drives demand not only for conventional data center-grade processors, but also for workstation-class CPUs used in smaller departmental AI servers.

Shipments of x86 CPUs declined both sequentially and year-over-year in Q3 2026 to 68.93 million units as rising component prices weighed on client PC demand, while server CPU shipments grew more than 20% year-over-year.

Intel regained overall x86 CPU market share from AMD for the first time since Q2 2025, largely thanks to a spectacular comeback in the desktop CPU segment, where its share reached 70.1%. Meanwhile, AMD gained 0.3% of the mobile CPU market, now commanding 29.2%, its highest share ever. Furthermore, AMD reached a record unit share in the server CPU segment, where it now commands 35.5%.

Both companies expect client CPU shipments to drop by more than 20% sequentially in Q4, whereas demand for server processors continues to grow due to the ongoing buildout of AI infrastructure.

@MKBHD It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.November 14, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that air travelers in the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents.
  • In a recent development, the problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that air travelers in the U.S. were in for a nasty surprise last Friday night after the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) called for a nationwide ground stop. According to the Wall Street Journal, the glitch started after a newly installed Juniper router, built by HP Enterprise, started broadcasting to a wide part of the network. This, in turn, overloaded the established and antiquated system, resulting in communications glitches and interruptions between air traffic control and pilots.

Sources indicate that thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents. Still, air traffic’s inability to communicate with high-flying aircraft made it impossible to coordinate the thousands of airborne aircraft at any given time, forcing the agency to call for an emergency ground stop. A nationwide ground stop order is quite a drastic move, and it has only been invoked twice before. The first such event was on September 11, 2001, when terrorists infamously used hijacked airliners as weapons. The second was on January 11, 2023, when the agency’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which sends warnings to pilots and air crews of important information crucial to flight safety, suffered from an outage for about a couple of hours.

In a recent development, the problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews. The agency then went on a nationwide hunt for the glitch, and it soon found two possible sources — an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Upon deeper inspection, the agency discovered that upcoming routers recently installed in both places have begun sending out a high volume of data across the entire FAA communications network.

It has been revealed that “We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds,” FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy stated in a press conference. This might seem like a minor hiccup for any modern network, which could typically handle connections in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions, per second. For example, one of the largest recorded DDoS attacks for 2026 saw traffic spike to 31.4 TB/s, which is enough to takedown an entire country’s web infrastructure.

However, the FAA still uses an antiquated copper network, which was easily overwhelmed by the amount of data that the routers sent. This network is already several decades old, so the agency is currently in the process of upgrading everything to fiber, which is costing taxpayers billions of dollars. Even as the agency is in this period of transition, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has raised several questions. “Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of router technology that we put into this system that propagated these errors?” Bedford said in statement on Saturday. He also added that the agency is investigating the incident. As for the Juniper router, an HPE spokesperson said that they appear to be working as intended and that “They did not fail.” It was eventually discovered that a specific feature on the router caused the system overload, with FAA employees turning it off across the entire network on all Juniper routers.

In a recent development, it took about four hours for the FAA to return its communications network to normal, but repercussions go way beyond that. Passengers aboard all those canceled and diverted flights needed to be served, even as latest passengers kept on arriving for their scheduled flights. It’s been estimated that airlines needed a few days to recover after the CrowdStrike crash of 2024 forced United, Delta, and American Airlines to cancel flights (except for Southwest, which avoided the chaos because it used an antiquated OS from the 1990s), so we expect passengers unlucky enough to be in transit during this incident to suffer waits between a few hours to a day or two before their journeys could continue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith have explained what they think defines a great video game soundtrack, in particular, a James Bond score.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the pair also discussed how they adapted their signature synth and acoustic hybrid styles to fit the traditional Bond aesthetic, Henson said, "We always look out for modern, thematic scores, with a unique take on action genres," to work with.

The Bond theme is one of the most iconic pieces of cinema music of all time, with Smith saying the music "must make the player feel like they are inhabiting the universe of James Bond.".

"A James Bond score has to have all those escapist elements we talked about before," Smith stated, referring to "spy craft, intrigue, action and romance.".

As for a memorable game score in general, Smith said the overall vibe needs to transport the player into the narrative and make it feel believable.

"A great game score should make the player feel like they are part of the story; giving atmosphere to the locations, humanity to the characters, and developing as they play through the story, the interactivity hidden but powerful," he explained.

The musical duo, known as The Flight, also believe that a score is another means to emphasise a game's story, with Smith saying, "A score needs to enrich and intensify the story and heighten emotional or exciting moments in the game.".

He added, "The music should also galvanise the player to move forwards and keep them entertained without being draining or too overwhelming.".

Henson continued, saying characters and locations always have their own recurring themes, which not only bolster the narrative, but also "gives familiarity" to the player.

"Game stories are likely to be completed over a matter of weeks rather than in one sitting," he said, "so this is even more key to get the player rapidly back into the world after some days out.".

In the same interview, Henson and Smith explained how a young James Bond was "harder than it looks" because they had to avoid using iconic melodies before the player earned his 007 status.

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nvidia Board Director Mark Stevens sold about 4.2 million of his shares, netting him around $1 billion in cash, almost exactly two months before Jensen Huang was accused of having “close ties” to an alleged Chinese spy.
  • Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million.
