📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nvidia Board Director Mark Stevens sold about 4.2 million of his shares, netting him around $1 billion in cash, almost exactly two months before Jensen Huang was accused of having “close ties” to an alleged Chinese spy. According to Moneywise.com, Stevens started the sale from August 31 to September 2, when Nvidia stock hovered between $220 and $226, which made him $411 million. The next tranche, totaling $236 million, came in the next couple of days as Nvidia traded from $227 to $234. The final sale happened on September 18 at around $220 per share, making Stevens approximately $300 million. These three transactions would have made him somewhere around $947 million.

Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million. However, unlike Stevens, who had no blueprint, this move was confirmed six months earlier in a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan to help avoid accusations of insider trading.

Nvidia’s stock price has taken a beating since the scandal broke, with the tech giant trading at $162.85 at the time of writing, its lowest level in the past 12 months. When the story first broke at the end of October, Nvidia shares were at around $205. It then started sliding, with the price at $178.67 after Jensen admitted to the affair last Sunday, although he did not name the involved party.

A second affair was revealed a few days after the former Nvidia chief’s confession, leading to his resignation from the company a few hours after that. The news sent Nvidia stock down to $151.09 — a nearly 25% drop from before the scandal. It recovered somewhat after the initial shock, climbing to nearly $170 before Friday’s trading, but took a beating again soon after the market opened.

Industry observers note that despite the sale, Stevens still holds about 27.5 million Nvidia shares, making him the second-largest shareholder after Jensen and Lori Huang. The price difference between today and September 18 is around $57, meaning he would have lost 25% of the value if he had sold after the scandal broke. Furthermore, his remaining Nvidia shares have lost more than $1.5 billion in value in just one quarter. Still, selling one’s holdings in a manufacturer as a board director does not constitute a crime. After all, it's unlikely that one could have predicted how hard Jensen Huang would fall in such a short time.

#475. Gamers may hate AI, but some are hooked on DLSS 5 — here's why that matters

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1519 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Gamers may hate AI, but some are hooked on DLSS 5 — here's why that matters

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Things are happening real fast in the gaming world ever since AI began advancing at a rapid pace throughout this year.
  • But from the flames of what appeared to be a complete PR wreckage with that initial reveal, DLSS 5 has emerged as a graphical phoenix.
  • This thread illustrates what I mean, in which the original poster wrote: "I'm getting too used to DLSS 5 graphics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Things are happening real fast in the gaming world ever since AI began advancing at a rapid pace throughout this year. Emulation is taking huge strides for one thing, and on the PC front, DLSS 5 has made a major splash. Although as you may recall, when Nvidia debuted the feature, it was almost universally shot down.

But from the flames of what appeared to be a complete PR wreckage with that initial reveal, DLSS 5 has emerged as a graphical phoenix. The turnaround in opinion was slow at first, but sentiment has shifted notably since NBA 2K27 showcased the tech to great effect, and now there are comments appearing on Reddit indicating that 'wow' moments are happening. 'I can't live without this' moments, in fact.

This thread illustrates what I mean, in which the original poster wrote: "I'm getting too used to DLSS 5 graphics. WOW factor is fading out. Turning it off looks flat like low graphics settings. It's just my new normal. How spoiled am I?".

Okay, so the Redditor is also observing that said 'wow' factor is fading, but in the respect that it's a upcoming normal — and going back to non-DLSS 5 visuals now feels horrible.

A replying Redditor agreed: "Spoiled. Every game feels like a remaster and indeed ultra settings with DLSS 5 off feel like the latest low settings. It's a new world and I'm loving it.".

Sources indicate that someone else chipped in: "It really feels that way and especially NPC faces. With DLSS 5 they get very natural looking skin and shadows in the right places and with it off, the face returns to a pale, shadowless, clay sculpture. It's jarring".

Want another? This gamer said: "Cyberpunk 2077 was the real eye opener for me. I crashed my game by installing a couple hundred mods. When I got it back again, I spent an hour frustrated trying to figure out why everybody looked so fake and plastic and cartoony. Turns out, ReShade had just stopped running in the background, and DLSS 5 had turned off.".

There are lots of observations like this, including that playing with DLSS 5 for a while and then going back to normal graphics is equivalent to getting used to 60fps (frames per second) gaming, and then having to return to 30fps. Some people feel that strongly about what they're getting here.

In case of any confusion, I should make it clear that these are gamers who are fudging DLSS 5 to work with unsupported games using various tools (and running it with older-gen Nvidia GPUs for that matter — it's only officially supported by RTX 5000 models). And yes, there's a definite caveat with this approach in that you need to be careful about how you're implementing the tech (there are various settings to adjust, and it's quite possible to go too over-the-top).

Industry observers note that even the most obvious drawback — the performance hit with DLSS 5 — is not ruining the graphical glow-up for gamers here, although admittedly it helps that the most pronounced benefits are being witnessed in older games (where base frame rates are a lot higher in general, with more headroom to take a hit, especially with a decent contemporary GPU). Nvidia is improving performance at a rate of knots, too, and the early honing work on DLSS 5 has been impressive indeed.

In a recent development, it's interesting to see just how much DLSS 5 is now swaying gamers who are experimenting with the tech, and I'll bet that while all this is an unofficial use of Nvidia's neural rendering trickery, Team Green is pleased to see this feedback in the midst of GPU price hikes rapidly reaching fresh and frightening peaks. (Not to mention that any good news will be welcome given the blow the manufacturer has suffered this week with the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, but that's another story — albeit one I think gamers should very much take note of).

In a recent development, lately, we've seen the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti spiral upwards in cost (along with other unpleasant increases down the GeForce range), and with further price rises pretty much inevitable — which are predicted to be potentially huge — the mentioned GPUs could end up something like triple their MSRPs in some countries by the end of the year. It really isn't a pleasant thought, and apparently Nvidia has cancelled the rumored RTX 5080 Super according to fresh gossip this week.

Industry observers note that that leaves the top-end of the GeForce GPU range as very much a high-and-dry place, with the RTX 5090 having more or less disappeared, the RTX 5080 now priced out of reach of everyone but the rich PC enthusiast, and the theorized additional graphics card not coming anymore. (If it ever was, although there have been plenty of rumors about the Super refresh that it's believable enough this was in Nvidia's looks at some point).

I don't think the GPU world has looked as bleak for a long time (AMD's Radeon graphics cards are afflicted by their own nasty hikes, too, with the manufacturer now thinking very much like Nvidia). So, what am I driving at here? A theory that Nvidia is pushing so hard with DLSS 5 because the company knows that it's vital given the RAM crisis and GPU price spikes, which I feel are going to become even more ludicrous next year.

Recent findings suggest that to go back to the Reddit thread I linked to above, another gamer observed: "We are all spoiled now. Just in time for all the hardware to evaporate.".

That's the hammer hitting the nail square-on as far as I'm concerned, but I think that Nvidia feels able to let the consumer side of its GPU hardware business slide more (with all those AI data center profits to be reaped), because it expects the software side to pick up the slack to an extent.

Industry observers note that if the performance tuning of DLSS 5 continues — which, of course, it will, and we'll surely see more major leaps in performance next year — the tech should be able to pep up lower-tier RTX 5000 GPUs quite nicely. In other words, the graphics cards which should remain in stock without a price tag that blows a ridiculous hole in your wallet (although I expect further pricing pain even at the budget-friendly end of the spectrum, make no mistake).

Industry observers note that okay, so it's true enough that diminishing returns are bound to kick in when the lower-hanging fruit for the honing and optimization of DLSS 5 is all picked, but I don't think that'll start to happen for some time yet. And don't forget that Nvidia is bringing support to RTX 4000 GPUs next year (I'm guessing sooner rather than later) to broaden the scope and effect of this technology considerably (though as noted, gamers are already doing this via workarounds).

With DLSS 5 quickly gaining more acceptance — and some gamers seemingly not able to play without it, even at this stage (with others going to great lengths to get it working with a PS5 for GTA 6, even) — it makes some sense that Nvidia is putting a lot of eggs in the neural rendering basket. Given how all this is unfolding, DLSS 5 might be Team Green's contingency plan if the GPU crisis becomes even more unbearable next year, tiding things over with software until the hardware situation improves.

Which ironically would mean that AI could be Nvidia's savior for the graphics card supply problems that were caused by AI in the first place (when it vacuumed up data center GPUs).

Sources indicate that remember that the original DLSS, when it was just upscaling, was not well-received when it first launched — and now look at it. I think DLSS 5 will likely go the same way, and indeed arguably it already has in the PC modding scene — at a breakneck pace — and I don't think it's a stretch to say it's likely going to be critical for Nvidia in the future, and especially next year.

  • According to recent reports, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable fresh warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA.
  • In a recent development, during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

According to recent reports, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable fresh warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

In a recent development, during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” said a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog says three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

After the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

It was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger.”.

In a recent development, this exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

After five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

It has been revealed that testers reckon the UGV packs are ready for deployment and use in “a host of other missions, including food, ammunition and supply logistics and more,” according to the DARPA blog. More UGV pack hunting tests are scheduled for December, with a group of serving soldiers involved.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Tribit FlyBuds C3 are a good set of wireless earbuds, with impressive sound quality for the money, strong EQ options, and a comfortable fit. However, their underwhelming battery life and plasticky build slightly hold them back. And while they’re temptingly cheap, their limited ANC is the one thing that stops me from recommending them over similarly priced rivals.

Good sound quality with powerful bass.

Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

Sources indicate that these aren’t just any earbuds, they’re FlyBuds. And the upcoming Tribit FlyBuds 3 look mighty impressive at a glance, especially when you consider their temptingly low price tag.

The Tribit FlyBuds 3 bring active noise cancellation, highly customizable EQ, and a six-microphone system for 'clear' voice calls. Sounds pretty good for $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60), right? But just how good are the FlyBuds C3? I’ve been using them for a couple of weeks now, and this is my verdict.

Sources indicate that first up, let’s talk about features. The Tribit FlyBuds C3 offer a lot of the functionality you’d expect from the best wireless earbuds.

Sources indicate that perhaps the main thing is ANC, which has five levels of strength, and can apparently block sounds “up to 45dB”. I have to say, though, that ANC on the FlyBuds C3 is disappointing. On walks, the sounds of nearby chatter and vehicles passing by were dulled, but still pretty audible. And when working in the office, the noise of typing was still pretty clear, even with my music at about 70% volume.

Again, the ANC here will certainly dull your surroundings, but it won’t block them out entirely. With that said, there is a very effective ambient mode that helps you stay aware of your environment when listening to tunes or taking phone calls on the go.

Industry observers note that most of the other features here did impress me, though. You get pretty detailed EQ options, with a number of presets for specific genres and use cases, as well as a full 10-band equalizer if you’re looking for more granular control. In addition, there’s a low-latency game mode, multi-point connectivity, and a hearing protection option.

Something else I appreciated about the FlyBuds C3 was their inclusion of customizable touch controls. By disabling single touch commands, and mapping playback controls to double taps (as well as ANC alterations to press and hold), I was able to avoid accidentally triggering unwanted button presses. You can map specific controls to each individual bud too, which is a great touch.

I also found the mic quality here to be plenty good enough. When taking phone calls and making a recording, I found that my speech was replicated accurately — I didn’t have to put up with the almost ‘underwater’ quality that some cheap models can apply. I picked up a bit of sibilance, and the microphones’ ability to carve out background noise was pretty limited, but in my view the call quality here is adequate for the price.

In a recent development, there are a few areas that could be improved, though. The X-3D spatial mode just makes music sound louder and less refined, there’s no wear detection or higher-res audio codec support, and the battery life here is surprisingly average.

Yes, you get just five hours from the buds with ANC active and seven hours without noise cancelling on, with up to 35 hours of playtime available with the case (with ANC off). A lot of Tribit’s budget audio tech goes big on battery, so I was expecting more here — that five hours with ANC on is especially weak when you consider you’ll need to use the standard EQ and keep volume at 50% or less to achieve it.

The FlyBuds C3 have been a bit of a mixed bag so far, but how do they fare when it comes to sound quality?

It has been revealed that let’s make a few things clear, though. These earbuds aren’t going to provide a wide, nuanced soundstage, impeccable detailing, or expert instrument separation. They can’t provide the quality that a pair of wired earbuds in this price-range, like the Sennheiser CX 80U can open up, for example, and keep things pretty basic. But you know what, they actually get those basics pretty spot on.

Industry observers note that they definitely emphasize the bass first, but this works to good effect. When tuning into Right Before My Eyes by N'n'G, the pounding low end hit with impressive depth and agility, without sounding muddy or unregimented. Vocals in the midrange weren’t particularly open or detailed, but they were relatively clear, and drums in the treble was articulate and snappy.

When listening to the 2020 remaster of Giant Steps by John Coltrane, I felt that instruments in the midrange sounded a touch recessed, but by giving them a bump with some EQ tweaks, they sounded clean and fairly expressive, and the keys were well-separated from the leading sax.

Overall, the FlyBuds C3 provide good sound for their price. Treble can get a little edgy at the higher volumes, and the mid-range needs a bit of tweaking to sound its best, but the powerful bass really shines here.

According to recent reports, in terms of design, the FlyBuds C3 keep it pretty simple, and that’s no bad thing. The earbuds themselves are small and lightweight, and are housed in a curved, ultra-compact charging case, making them perfect for sliding into your pocket. While the buds do have a plasticky and cheap-looking appearance, this can be forgiven for the price, and they do look curved and fairly stylish in-use, whether you go for the black or white color variant.

Industry observers note that you also get small, medium, and large ear tips in the box, enabling you to find the perfect fit. For me, the medium ear tips were spot on, and I found the C3 to be very comfortable in use, with no signs of fatigue after a full day’s use. IP55 waterproofing also makes these safe to use when working out or listening in light rain.

Sources indicate that the Tribit FlyBuds C3 sound pretty solid for the price, offer decent comfort, and have pretty generous EQ options. However, the models I’ve added in the ‘also consider’ section — the Nothing Ear (a) and JLab Go Pods ANC — deliver better ANC while still offering good sound quality. So, if you can get one of those models at a similar price to the C3, you might get better bang for your buck.

It has been revealed that the Tribit FlyBuds C3 were released in September 2026, about five years after their predecessor, the FlyBuds C2 hit the market. The C3 deviate from the C2 pretty drastically, offering a proper in-ear seal, as well as active noise cancellation capabilities.

With a list price of $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60), the Tribit FlyBuds C3 sit firmly in the budget category. Rivals include the CMF Buds Pro 2, the Earfun Air 2, and the Sony WF-C510.

5 hours (buds with ANC on); 8 hours (buds, with ANC off); up to 35 hours (with charging case).

Great EQ options and solid call quality, but ANC and battery life underwhelm.

You want super-comfortable earbudsI found the C3 to be very comfortable in use, and they come with multiple-sized eartips, helping you to get the perfect fit for long listening sessions.

Recent findings suggest that I spent two weeks testing the Tribit FlyBuds C3, taking them everywhere with me — to the office, on public transport, and on walks. Testing them out in a variety of environments helped me assess their ANC in full, as well as their transparency mode.

As always, I commenced testing by sifting through the TechRadar reference playlist, which features tracks from a variety of genres, but I also listened to hours worth of tunes from my personal library.

More generally, I’ve spent years testing audio gear here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

In a recent development, the enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. Recent findings suggest that the app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

Finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

#470. 3D printing dev’s free tool unlocks curved printing along all three axes

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (615 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

3D printing dev’s free tool unlocks curved printing along all three axes

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer.
  • Alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners.
  • Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Recent findings suggest that alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

Sources indicate that one of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Owners can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

While PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

5 Non-Hybrid 4-Cylinder Cars That Get Over 30 MPG

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with fuel prices out of control in the United States and worldwide, the smartest financial decision you can make before buying a new car is to pay close attention to its fuel efficiency.
  • It has been revealed that if you haven't been keeping tabs on automotive developments, car engines are getting smaller even as cars get bigger.
  • Recent findings suggest that as experts tracking the latest models on the market, we've done extensive research and identified five non-hybrid four-cylinder cars that meet this threshold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with fuel prices out of control in the United States and worldwide, the smartest financial decision you can make before buying a new car is to pay close attention to its fuel efficiency. Hybrid cars use an electric motor (or motors), making them far more efficient than gas-only models. That's why the most fuel-efficient cars you can buy often have hybrid powertrains. While hybrid cars are best known for their fuel-sipping tendencies, don't assume non-hybrid models can't deliver good fuel economy.

It has been revealed that if you haven't been keeping tabs on automotive developments, car engines are getting smaller even as cars get bigger. One advantage of this trend is that smaller engines tend to use less fuel, making non-hybrid cars more efficient. Although hybrid cars still lead in fuel efficiency, they are typically more expensive than their non-hybrid counterparts. Fortunately, some modern non-hybrid vehicles now come with fuel-efficient four-cylinder engines that can achieve more than 30 miles per gallon, making them appealing options for those looking to cut fuel costs.

Recent findings suggest that as experts tracking the latest models on the market, we've done extensive research and identified five non-hybrid four-cylinder cars that meet this threshold. Each model had to deliver at least 30 mpg in combined city and highway driving, based on official U.S. Environmental Protection Agency figures.

It has been revealed that honda refreshed the Civic sedan for 2027, with the non-hybrid model powered by a highly efficient 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that produces 150 hp and 133 lb-ft of torque. The EPA estimates the non-hybrid Civic can deliver up to 32 mpg in the city, 41 mpg on the highway, and 36 mpg combined. The less-efficient Sport trim, with bigger 18-inch wheels, still delivers excellent fuel economy above 30 mpg.

EPA estimates rate the Honda Civic Sport trim at up to 31 mpg city, 39 mpg highway, and 34 mpg combined. With a 12.4-gallon fuel tank, a full tank can give you over 400 miles. Both non-hybrid variants use a continuously variable transmission (CVT) and send power to the front wheels. The Civic Sedan's sticker price makes it even more attractive. Both the Sport and LX variants start under $30,000.

To get your hands on the 2027 Honda Civic sedan, you'll need to spend at least $26,290, including a $1,295 destination charge, for the base LX trim. The Civic Sport sedan starts at an MSRP of $26,995, or $28,290 with the destination charge.

Hyundai's 2026 compact Elantra sedan is also very fuel-efficient. According to official EPA ratings, the Elantra delivers up to 31 mpg city, 40 mpg highway, and 35 mpg combined. It's available in six trims, and the numbers vary slightly by trim. For example, the SEL Sport Premium variant is rated to offer up to 30 mpg in the city, 40 mpg on the highway, and 34 mpg combined.

Sources indicate that for the best fuel economy, choose the base SE trim, the most efficient across the board. Fortunately, all gas variants of the Elantra deliver over 30 mpg combined, including the sporty Elantra N Line, which uses a more powerful turbocharged engine. Except for the sporty N Line variant, all gas trims of the 2026 Elantra use a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that makes 147 ponies and 132 lb-ft of torque.

It has been revealed that the N Line variant has a 1.6-liter turbocharged inline-4 that makes 201 hp and 195 lb-ft of torque. All Elantra variants send power to the front wheels by default. The Hyundai Elantra is even more pocket-friendly, starting at $24,120, including a $1,295 destination charge. The Elantra N Line is the only gas trim that exceeds $30,000.

Sources indicate that one of the best-selling Toyota models in the company's history, the Corolla has been in production for ages. The 2027 Toyota Corolla marks the 60th anniversary of the nameplate. While the Japanese automaker has released a special hybrid edition to celebrate the milestone, the regular gas-powered Corolla is also fuel-efficient. It's another example that you don't need a hybrid to get fuel efficiency figures over 30 mpg.

The EPA rates the 2027 Corolla at over 30 mpg in all scenarios. The LE trim gets the highest rating: 32 mpg city, 41 mpg highway, and 35 mpg combined, while the XSE and SE variants deliver up to 31 mpg city, 40 mpg highway, and 34 mpg combined. Among other factors, the Toyota Corolla's secret sauce for its excellent fuel economy is a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that produces 169 hp and 151 lb-ft of torque and drives only the front wheels via a CVT.

It has been revealed that the base LE trim rides on 16-inch wheels, while the XSE and SE models use bigger 18-inch all-season tires. The 2027 Corolla LE, the lineup's base trim, starts at $24,620, including the mandatory $1,295 processing and handling fee. Moving up the lineup, the SE variant starts at $27,060, while the top-tier XSE trim starts at $30,335, including the mandatory handling fee.

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 Volkswagen Jetta is another solid option if you want to avoid hybrids and still get fuel efficiency over 30 mpg. However, not every Jetta trim can deliver over 30 mpg. Available in five trims, the Jetta has an EPA rating of up to 29 mpg city, 40 mpg highway, and 34 mpg combined. Those numbers apply to the base S trim; the Sport, SE, and SEL models are rated up to 29 mpg city, 40 mpg highway, and 33 mpg combined.

It has been revealed that the S, Sport, SE, and SEL trims share the same powertrain: a 1.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine producing 158 hp and 184 lb-ft of torque, paired with an eight-speed automatic transmission. The company credits some of the engine's fuel efficiency to early intake valve closure during the induction stroke. However, as mentioned earlier, not every 2027 Jetta trim delivers combined EPA ratings over 30 mpg.

It has been revealed that you'll want to avoid the fully specced GLI model the company says is targeted for the Autobahn, as it has an EPA rating of 26 mpg city, 35 mpg highway, and 29 mpg combined. The 2027 Volkswagen Jetta S has a starting MSRP of $23,995, which comes to $25,320 with the $1,325 destination charge.

The 2027 Nissan Sentra features a fuel-efficient, four-cylinder, gas-only engine with an EPA-estimated maximum combined rating of 33 mpg. The Sentra is powered by a 2.0-liter inline-four engine available in all grades, producing 149 hp and 146 lb-ft of torque and paired with a CVT. The S, SV, and SL grades lead the 2027 Sentra in fuel efficiency, rated up to 30 mpg city, 38 mpg highway, and 33 mpg combined.

The top-tier SR takes a slight fuel-economy hit but still delivers over 30 mpg, with an EPA-estimated rating of 29 mpg city, 36 mpg highway, and 32 mpg combined. It might not seem like much compared to other models we've discussed; however, that makes the Nissan Sentra quite fuel-efficient and, surprisingly, it even outperforms some hybrid models, including the 2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Hybrid, rated at 27 mpg city, 27 mpg highway, and 27 mpg combined.

In a recent development, the entry-level S grade of the 2027 Nissan Sentra starts at an MSRP of $24,265, including a $1,275 destination and handling charge. The SV costs $25,265, while the SR and SL start at $26,265 and $29,265, respectively, with the destination fee included.

#467. How A Lawn Mower Mulching Plug Might Save You Valuable Time This Fall

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (498 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

How A Lawn Mower Mulching Plug Might Save You Valuable Time This Fall

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As fall turns to winter, some homeowners are transitioning from just cutting the grass to mulching the yard.
  • A mulching plug, depending on its design, can be a cover that attaches to your mower's grass chute.
  • It has been revealed that you can add a mulching plug to many push mowers and riding mowers, and you have options when it comes to style, as designs can vary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As fall turns to winter, some homeowners are transitioning from just cutting the grass to mulching the yard. While you can use a mulching lawn mower to do this work, you could also do it with a standard lawn mower, provided you have the right setup. That setup can include a mulching plug, which could save you some time in the long run.

A mulching plug, depending on its design, can be a cover that attaches to your mower's grass chute. The cover keeps the grass clippings from shooting out of the mower and spreading over the yard. Instead, the clippings stay under the mower, where they're repeatedly cut into smaller pieces. Of course, if you're cutting leaves instead of raking them, they will also become part of the mulch you're making. This way, you can get your mulching done as you mow versus having to do it after the fact.

It has been revealed that you can add a mulching plug to many push mowers and riding mowers, and you have options when it comes to style, as designs can vary. For example, if you're working with a riding mower, you could choose a mulching plug that connects under the deck around the blade or on the rear chute. Additionally, you can search for a plug that's made specifically for your mower brand, like John Deere or Craftsman. You can also shop for third-party options that fit your mower as well.

Toro recommends regularly cleaning the mulching plug to prevent buildup that could affect overall performance. But before you remove the plug, be sure your lawn mower is turned off, the blades have stopped moving, and the spark plug wire is disconnected. It's also a good idea to refer to your owner's manuals for maintenance guidelines specific to your mulching plug and lawn mower.

According to recent reports, using a mulching plug on your mower, especially if you're cutting leaves, can have a lasting positive impact on your yard. That's because the mulch you're leaving behind is actually helping to build a safe and productive environment for birds, insects, and other animals. Mulching leaves also enriches the ground and can improve the health of your grass over time. It can even reduce the number of weeds that may pop up later on.

Industry observers note that however, there are some things you should know about mulching before you decide to do it. First, you shouldn't mulch when the ground is wet, as it could result in a mess of clumped grass wherever you mow. This could affect your yard's appearance while also preventing the grass from getting the oxygen and sunshine it needs. If the grass you're mulching is too tall, that can also be a problem, as it can create a matted layer that just sits on top of your lawn. Additionally, if your yard is already unhealthy with diseased areas, then mulching those spots means you could be expanding the problem.

#466. Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (554 w)
Gadgets 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware

Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed.
  • It has been revealed that micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is.
  • The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some new evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the big three memory chip manufacturers.

It has been revealed that micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”.

The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was rapidly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also noted that the three companies declared the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”.

Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

The significant three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also mentioned that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

In a recent development, despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.

Sources indicate that the Samsung S85H is great entry-level OLED TV that can compete with the best TVs of 2026. It offers a near-full feature set, with brilliant performance at a competitive price. While its closest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper at the moment, and arguably the better buy — as I found when I compared it and the S85H side-by-side — this is still a very capable TV.

Sources indicate that the S85H’s picture quality is excellent overall. It delivers punchy, vibrant colors, strong contrast, crisp, realistic textures and good motion handling. It does have a reflective screen, an issue the step-up Samsung S90H doesn’t suffer from, and there are sometimes black-crush issues in darker scenes, but the S85H’s picture is competitive with the best OLED TVs.

In a recent development, sound quality in the S85H is a mixed bag. It has great accuracy, and at times punchy bass, but generally its limited two-channel speaker system can only do so much. Sound feels contained to the back of the screen, and while there is some extension beyond the TV’s frame, it doesn’t offer what one of the best soundbars could. It’s fine for day-to-day viewing, but you’ll want a soundbar if you’re after a more cinematic experience.

For gaming, the S85H is a fantastic budget-OLED option. It has a suite full of features up there with the best gaming TVs — 4K 120Hz, FreeSync and G-Sync, HDR10+ gaming and ALLM — as well as ultra-low input lag and four HDMI 2.1 ports. Its performance is responsive and smooth, and it serves as a superb gaming TV.

Industry observers note that the S85H is good value for money. The 55-inch model I tested costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, putting it in the more affordable OLED bracket. While its nearest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper ($799 / £999 / AU$1,699 for the 55-inch), making it the better-value buy, the S85H still offers brilliant performance and features for the price, and that price is only going to get cheaper.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung S85H is the entry-level model in Samsung’s 2026 OLED TV lineup, sitting below the mid-range S90H and flagship S95H/S99H. It’s available in sizes 48-83-inch, with the 55-inch model I tested launching for $1,499 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 in May-June 2026 (depending on region).

Since its release, the S85H’s prices have dropped across all sizes and in all regions. The 55-inch is now available (November 2026) for around $999 / £999 / AU$1,899, though you can find it for less at some retailers in some regions. The rival LG B6 55-inch is cheaper at the moment in the US and Australia, costing $799 / £999 / AU$1,699, but it’s likely that the ‘cheaper’ title will change hands a few times during these TV’s life cycles.

Sources indicate that the S85H uses a WOLED panel, the same one as in the rival LG B6 and the same as the step-up S90H, though some sizes are reported to have QD-OLED. The S90H benefits from the upgraded NQ4 AI Gen 3 Processor, which allows for higher brightness and better color performance, while the S85H has the older NQ4 AI Gen 2 Processor built in. The Gen 2 is no slouch, though, and supports picture features such as 4K AI Upscaling and Real Depth Enhancer Pro.

The S85H supports HDR10+, including the new HDR10+ Advanced, HDR10 and HLG HDR formats, but as usual with Samsung TVs, there’s no support for Dolby Vision.

In a recent development, for audio, the S85H has a 2-channel, 20W speaker system with support for Dolby Atmos. A number of AI sound features are included too, such as AI Sound Pro, as well as Object Tracking Sound (OTS) Lite. Q-Symphony, where the TV’s speakers can be used in conjunction with a supported Samsung soundbar, is also featured.

The S85H supports 4K 120Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming, which works across all of the S85H’s four HDMI 2.1 ports. There’s also a Game Hub, where cloud gaming apps are housed.

In a recent development, tizen serves as the S85H’s smart TV platform, supporting all major streaming apps such as Netflix and Disney Plus. Tizen also features the Vision AI companion, which uses multiple AI agents to make content and even lifestyle recommendations you may ask such as recommended places for dinner.

In a recent development, as the S85H uses a standard WOLED panel, its brightness doesn’t match that of step-up OLEDs like the S90H or LG C6. In my testing it clocked a peak HDR brightness (on a 10% window pattern) of 833 nits and 854 nits in Filmmaker Mode and Standard respectively. Those scores put it in line with the rival LG B6E (which hit 808 nits and 727 nits in the same respective modes), but are much lower than those achieved by the step-up S90H, which measured 1,689 and 1677 in the same two modes.

As for fullscreen brightness, the S85H hit just over 150 nits in both Filmmaker and Standard, which is about right for WOLED, but it’s still a significant drop compared to rival mini-LEDs such as the TCL QM7L/C7L, which hit over 600 nits. This means the S85H can struggle in bright rooms, and without an effective anti-glare coating, dark scenes can be hard to watch in brighter conditions, so this TV is best suited to viewing in ambient or dark conditions. Samsung’s step-up S90H OLED, on the other hand, easily handles bright rooms.

Sources indicate that starting with SDR content, the S85H does a good job of upscaling textures. Watching various programs on Samsung TV Plus, textures did look cleaner and sharpened than you’d get on some standard LED and mini-LED TVs, and with bolder colors. While the step-up S90H did a better job with upscaling, the S85H’s was still impressive nonetheless.

Switching to 4K HDR content, the S85H delivers excellent colors. Watching Elemental on Disney Plus in HDR10+, the bold oranges of the fire people and blues of the water people pop throughout the movie, even in the slightly dimmer Filmmaker Mode. Putting the S85H in Movie mode adds more brightness and a bit more color depth which works well for the animation. As Ember runs across multi-colored minerals, colors have a nice shine to them, showing the S85H’s punchy HDR highlights.

Watching a live-action movie, The Sound of Music, the S85H indicates it can render realistic-looking colors too. The green fields and blue skies of Austria look wonderfully natural whenever they’re on screen, and the S85H shows true-to-life skin tones in the people as well.

Measuring the S85H’s HDR color-gamut coverage, it registered 97.9% of the UHDA-P3 and 73.4% of the BT.2020 color spaces. These numbers are about right for a WOLED TV, but are starting to fall behind those of more premium OLEDs and RGB mini-LED TVs. Still the S85H’s colors were great overall.

The S85H also demonstrates strong contrast. In The Batman, which includes lots of scenes with lights cutting through the dark environments, such as in the Batcave and in aerial shots of Gotham, the S85H shows an excellent balance between these light and dark tones to create an authentic image. The same is true in Project Hail Mary, with both shots of space and scenes inside the ship showing the S85H’s powerful contrast and deep black levels.

It has been revealed that shadow detail is also great, with details and textures legible in challenging dark scenes, such as frames on the wall of Mayor Mitchell’s house in The Batman. I did notice during some particularly dark shots that the S85H was prone to some black crush, even in pitch-black viewing conditions. For the most part however, its contrast was impressive.

The S85H also demonstrated crisp textures in nearly every scene I watched, with people in particular looking true-to-life. This 3D-like level of detail was one of the S85H’s strengths over the LG B6E when I tested the two side-by-side, showcasing the effectiveness of the Real Depth Enhancer feature.

Industry observers note that finally, the S85H demonstrated very good motion for both sports and movies, although some setup is required. I found setting blur reduction to 3 and judder reduction between 3-5 (depending on the content and how fluid you want your picture) was the most effective. There were still some motion artefacts when watching a soccer match on Prime Video, with some blurring of textures in some shots, but the S85H was mostly effective.

The S85H’s two-channel, 20W speaker system isn’t strong enough to allow you to skimp on a soundbar if you want powerful and immersive sound for action-heavy movies and shows, and doesn’t match up to step-up TVs, but is mostly fine for day-to-day viewing and some movies.

It has been revealed that watching the Batmobile scene from The Batman, the S85H’s strength lay in the accuracy of sound, showing how effective the OTS Lite system was. As the Batmobile swerved through traffic, screeching tires and car horns were mapped with real accuracy between the sound and action on the screen.

Impacts also generated some nice punch. As the Batmobile clatters through a barricade, the sound of scraping metal had some weight to it, and as the Batmobile’s engine revved, there was some punchy bass. However, when I pushed the volume, the bass did seem to fizzle out, and high-end sound could be a little harsh.

Sources indicate that while I did hear some extension of sound from the frame of the screen, particularly during the aforementioned swerving manoeuvres, the sound felt contained to the rear of the screen, making it feel like the viewing experience was lacking some depth. Speech was mostly clear throughout, but could get lost at times. Again, you want a cinematic experience, I’d hook up a soundbar.

In a recent development, the most striking thing visually about the S85H is how thin it is compared to rival TVs in this price range. It has a sleek, metal frame and a razor-thin depth that suggest a more premium price. Even its rear panel is fairly trim, with only a small bump to accommodate the connection ports.

Industry observers note that for the 55-inch model I tested, two plastic feet were supplied which, while they felt a little cheap, were very easy to install. You can choose between two positions for the feet, narrow and wide, with the latter being very useful if you have a soundbar. The TV is also very light for a 55-inch model, but still felt sturdy when placed on a TV stand.

It has been revealed that the S85H comes with Samsung’s SolarCell remote, which offers solar and USB-C charging. Its small size means it could get lost quite easily, but it feels light in the hand, and offers all the usual options (streaming app shortcuts, settings, power and volume).

Samsung’s own Tizen serves as the smart TV platform for the S85H, and with it come a host of AI features via the Vision AI companion, which uses AI agents to help with content recommendation, lifestyle advice, and more general questions you might ask of a smart assistant (how long is a day on Jupiter was one of the example prompts). There are also a host of AI Picture and sound features via the AI Mode settings (found under the Advanced Features menu), such as AI Soccer Mode and Adaptive Sound Pro.

Tizen’s main three hubs on the main screen — For You, Live, and Game and Apps — host recommended content, live TV, gaming content and a general apps page respectively. These pages are generally laid out well, but do have banner ads that take up about a third of the page. I also found Samsung TV Plus autoplays on the For You page and can sometimes take over the page if left idle, which can be frustrating.

You can choose from a good number of picture settings, all housed in logical places within the settings menu. Some of these settings, such as Auto HDR Remastering for SDR content, can be effective. Sound settings are a bit more limited, and I’d have liked more than two sound mode options. Tizen is a solid interface overall, but doesn’t quite match up to LG’s webOS or Roku for ease-of-use.

In a recent development, the S85H is an excellent choice for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, perfect for multiple consoles, and all of these support 4K 120Hz, full VRR including FreeSync and G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming. The featured Game Hub is a useful home for all things gaming, and offers quick access to a connected console and cloud gaming apps.

Industry observers note that the S85H’s input lag registered 9.2ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.5ms at 1080p 120Hz, the latter of which is one of the lowest scores I’ve seen. This translates into actual gaming too. Playing Battlefield V, motion felt incredibly smooth with razor-sharp response times — extremely useful when faced with tons of enemies.

Picture-wise, the S85H’s brilliant quality is great for gaming. The colors of autumnal trees during one mission really popped on screen, while textures were very crisp, and, during night-time missions, black tones were deep and contrast was strong.

The 55-inch S85H I tested currently costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, which is very good for a budget OLED. Considering the features and performance it delivers, it’s great value for money overall.

According to recent reports, right now, its major rival, the LG B6, is cheaper in most places. A 55-inch LG B6 (or in some cases LG B6E, which isn’t markedly different from the standard B6) costs around $799 / £999 / AU$1,699. The B6 offers near-identical features and performance, so right now it’s the better deal.

It has been revealed that the Samsung S90H is a notable step-up over the S85H, offering higher brightness, better picture quality and an anti-reflection screen for bright-room viewing. The 55-inch model costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,999, so if you’re in the UK and US and can stretch your budget, it’s worth the upgrade. Still, the S85H is good value overall, and I expect its prices will drop and fall more in line with those of the B6 as time goes on.

You want OLED at a more affordable priceIf you're looking for an OLED TV but don't want to fork out the massive bucks, the S85H is a perfect gateway into the tech.

You want great picture quality The S85H thrives with colorful movies, but also presents strong contrast and crisp textures that highlight what's to love about OLED.

You want a gaming TVFully kitted out with four HDMI 2.1 ports and every feature you could need and the performance to go with it, the S85H is perfect for gaming.

Sources indicate that you need Dolby VisionThere's no support for Dolby Vision HDR, which is used on a lot of 4K Blu-rays and streaming services. This is the case with all Samsung TVs.

You want the best soundThe S85H's built-in sound is solid enough for day-to-day viewing, but if you want a more cinematic experience, you'll need a soundbar.

You can stretch your budget to the Samsung S90HIn some sizes, the step-up Samsung S90H is only a little pricier and its big upgrade over the S85H, with an anti-glare screen and higher brightness.

Industry observers note that dolby Vision, HDR10+. HDR10, HLG.

In a recent development, LG B6The LG B6 is the S85H's closest rival and offers similar performance and features, but for slightly cheaper. The B6 has richer colors and Dolby Vision, while the S85H has crisper textures. Both deliver strong contrast as well, and are full kitted out for gaming. This comes down to whichever model is cheaper.

Industry observers note that samsung S90HThe step-up model from the S85H, the S90H is pricier, but it has an effective anti-glare screen perfect for bright rooms, better picture quality and a better processor. The S90H is worth the investment if you can stretch your budget.

TCL QM7L/C7LThe TCL QM7L (US)/C7L (UK/Aus) is the brand's mid-range SDQ mini-LED. While the S85H delivers better contrast and textures, the QM7L/C7L is much brighter and offers competitive gaming features and performance for a similar price. Pick the QM7L/C7L if you have a brighter room.

Read our TCL QM7L review and TCL C7L review.

I first started my testing of the Samsung S85H with casual viewing to assess which picture mode was best, landing on Filmmaker and Movie modes for movies and TV and Standard for sports and broadcast TV.

I then tested the S85H using reference 4K Blu-ray, analyzing its color, contrast, textures and detail and motion, while also using SDR sports and daytime TV to analyze its upscaling capabilities.

Once these tests were complete, I took measurements using a Murido Six G 8K test pattern generator, a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer profiled with the a Klein K-10A colorimeter, and recorded the measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

I tested the S85H's brightness, measuring on a white window pattern in sizes 1-100%, with a focus on 10% peak and 100% fullscreen brightness, in both SDR and HDR.

I then measured its color and grayscale accuracy in SDR using Delta-E averages (the margin for error between the test pattern signal and what's displayed on screen).

Next was HDR color gamut coverage, where I sued the UHDA-P3 (the color space used for 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema releases) and BT.2020 (becoming more commonly used) color spaces.

It has been revealed that I also measured the S85H's HDR EOTF, using 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits targets, which demonstrates the TV's accuracy between light and dark tones. I also measured its Spectral Power Distribution, which measures its color performance.

Finally, I measured its input lag in both 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.

Recent findings suggest that honda uses Bose for the upgraded factory stereo in select versions of the Civic, Accord, CR-V, Passport, and Pilot. However, in less expensive Hondas, the audio system can have a very different setup. On models such as the Civic LX, for example, Honda lists the speaker count and amplifier power without naming any brand.

Also, even two vehicles in the same lineup and model year might have different stereos. For example, one of the biggest differences between the 2024 Honda Accord trims is that the Touring Hybrid came with Bose audio, while the Sport Hybrid and EX-L Hybrid had eight-speaker systems. So even if you've narrowed your search to a hybrid Accord, you could end up with a different sound system depending on which version you buy.

Once you're in the car, sound quality comes down to more than the speakers themselves. Honda audio might sound okay when you're parked, but on a highway it has to compete with voices and tire noise. So, the Bose upgrade can perform better in those conditions, especially when compared to the standard stereo.

Sources indicate that the 2026 Civic sedan has three factory audio setups. The LX starts with four speakers and 160 watts, while the Sport and Sport Hybrid double the speaker count and step up to 180 watts. However, Bose audio is standard only on the Sport Touring Hybrid, where the 12-speaker setup includes a dedicated subwoofer to handle the lowest notes.

Honda offered Bose in the 2023 Civic Sport Touring hatchback, which was one of the coolest features of that model. Some of the speakers sit in the rear roof pillars, with an eight-inch woofer tucked into a rear quarter panel. Bose's Dynamic Speed Compensation adjusts the tone and volume as the car speeds up, helping offset the extra noise at higher speeds.

Industry observers note that the Passport, however, tends to vary by model year. Honda listed ten speakers for the 2021 Elite car, but didn't name the audio brand. The 2026 TrailSport Elite does get a 12-speaker Bose system, so keep an eye on the model year and trim name when shopping for a used car.

In a recent development, honda's Bose upgrade sounds very good for a mainstream car or SUV. In our review of the 2026 Pilot Elite, we found that music stayed clear even with the volume all the way up. In the Civic, the upgrade also gets you a dedicated subwoofer, which TotallyEV found helped bring out more of the low end in a song.

In a recent development, the Civic's Bose stereo also stood out for its volume and clarity next to the Kia K4's Harman Kardon system in our side-by-side review. Toyota offers JBL in the 2026 Corolla XSE, and JBL and Harman Kardon are both part of Harman. Whether you prefer the Corolla's JBL stereo or the Civic's Bose system comes down to how the speakers are placed and tuned in each car.

Industry observers note that honda's luxury division, Acura, goes a step further with its stereo systems, coming with a 31-speaker Bang & Olufsen system in the 2026 MDX Type S Advance. The headliner has twelve speakers, so sound comes from above you as well as all around you, making it more immersive.

#463. What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (447 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

What Does A 'No Thru Trucks' Road Sign Mean?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds.
  • According to recent reports, as the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks.
  • In a recent development, let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most vehicles travel anywhere between 25 and 80 mph, so drivers should ideally be able to understand a road sign's meaning within two seconds. However, some traffic signs are confusing. Usually, these signs provide instructions for the road in the immediate vicinity, but one sign acts as a "do not enter" notification that only applies to specific drivers.

According to recent reports, as the first and final words imply, "No Thru Trucks" signs are meant to restrict road access for trucks. But what is a "Thru Truck" anyway? It isn't some obscure electric truck; it just means that trucks can't use the roads with this sign unless their destination is somewhere along the path. In other words, "No Thru Trucks" signs are just "Local Traffic Only" road signs designed specifically for commercial and construction trucks. You can usually find these signs in residential areas and near (but not necessarily on) highways.

In a recent development, let's construct an example to help you understand how these signs function. Say you are an Amazon delivery driver. You start your route in the warehouse with all your packages and while driving, you come across a street with a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Check what deliveries you need to make that day. If you don't have a package to deliver on that street or a street connected to it, you should find another route, no matter how much more time and gas it will require. If you are supposed to deliver a package there, you are allowed to enter the road.

It has been revealed that depending on where you drive, you could spend your entire life without seeing a "No Thru Trucks" sign. Instead, places might use alternatives, such as "No Trucks Except Local Deliveries" or "Commercial Vehicles Prohibited." Different song, same tune.

As a general rule of thumb, if you drive a commercial truck and ignore a "No Thru Trucks" sign without having a delivery in the area, you might face a fine and court time. The restrictions that dictate truck traffic are from local government, which sets up the signs and catches violators. And that's assuming the sign is installed in the correct location, because while it is rare, sometimes road workers make mistakes.

Even if a "No Thru Trucks" sign is placed seemingly in the middle of nowhere, many drivers follow its instructions anyway. Residents who are sick and tired of hearing trucks speed by their homes might request the sign's installation, so its presence is a regulation meant as a way to give people who live nearby some peace and quiet. Is that really so much to ask?

#461. Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (471 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running.
  • This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck. German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024, which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the matter wasn’t caught earlier.

This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still.

Industry observers note that aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few significant tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.

#460. Why a Galaxy AI paywall would drive me away from Samsung's AI features

Why a Galaxy AI paywall would drive me away from Samsung's AI features

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the more controversial aspects of Galaxy AI's 2024 launch (besides its uselessness) was that Samsung would only keep Galaxy AI free for a limited time.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, Samsung quietly postponed the December 2025 deadline, and Galaxy AI remained free for everyone.
  • A report from Sammy Guru revealed placeholder images and code strings that suggested Samsung is preparing and testing a upcoming AI Premium subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the more controversial aspects of Galaxy AI's 2024 launch (besides its uselessness) was that Samsung would only keep Galaxy AI free for a limited time.

Recent findings suggest that however, Samsung quietly postponed the December 2025 deadline, and Galaxy AI remained free for everyone. But recent reports indicate that Samsung is preparing an AI Premium subscription, and if Google's AI subscription is anything to go by, I guarantee I'll be using Galaxy AI less.

A report from Sammy Guru revealed placeholder images and code strings that suggested Samsung is preparing and testing a upcoming AI Premium subscription.

Recent findings suggest that this subscription will give Galaxy AI consumers more access to existing and new features. According to the reports, the free plan will include the following features, labeled as "Standard AI":.

In a recent development, currently, these features offer unlimited access, with a couple of small exceptions. However, when AI Premium launches, they will be subject to usage limits.

On top of extra usage, the premium subscription will grant access to the following features:.

A later report from SamMobile found that Samsung might be testing different subscription tiers.

Overall, it seems like Samsung is trying to recoup its losses by charging users. But when it's not offering much to begin with, why would anyone pay? Certainly not me.

It's been two years since Samsung graced us with Galaxy AI, and since then it has received a host of upgrades. But is it useful?

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Samsung revealed which AI tools in its Galaxy AI suite are the most popular. Ironically, the top feature was Circle to Search, a Google feature that Samsung can't lock behind a paywall.

The next most popular feature was Photo Assist, which appears on Samsung's list of "Standard AI" features it will add usage limits to.

Sources indicate that after you take a photo on a supported Galaxy phone, Photo Assist suggests a selection of edits to improve your photos. These suggestions can range from simple crops to generative AI tweaks.

The problem is that while these suggestions can be useful, Samsung slaps a visible watermark on any images it edits. You can implement the suggestions yourself, but there isn't much to them beyond what a basic photography guide can teach you.

Then there's Now Brief. It's impressive how Samsung has barely managed to improve this feature. Every time I see it, it tells me something like "It's raining. Bring an umbrella.".

Unless you live in a house without windows, its weather reports are completely irrelevant. Then there are the random news articles and health information. None of this information needs an AI to power it.

In short, Galaxy AI is a gimmick, and if I'm forced to pay to use it, I'll just stop using it altogether.

When I bought my Pixel 10 Pro last year, Google generously gave me a one-year trial of Google AI Pro.

Recent findings suggest that through this subscription, I got four times higher access to Gemini, plus access to Gemini 4 Argon and Deep Research. Then there was Gemini in Workspace apps, expanded access to Gemini Notebook, Google Flow, and more.

Nearly a year later, I use none of these features regularly, and I haven't come close to hitting the increased Gemini access.

Gemini has made a mess of summarizing my documents so many times that I'd rather pay Google not to show it while I'm working.

Samsung seems to be modeling its AI Premium subscription after Google's AI Pro prepares. But at the end of the day, all the useful features (like Circle to Search) remain free, and all the gimmicks are locked behind a paywall.

Google hasn't figured out how to add value to its AI prepares for everyday users, so what chance does Samsung have?

Samsung never revealed why it kept postponing the end of free Galaxy AI access, but I suspect it was to lock as many people in to using the features.

Recent findings suggest that the idea of getting people used to a free tier to encourage adoption of a paid feature is nothing upcoming. But when Galaxy AI is still such poor value, I certainly won't be paying Samsung a penny to use its "premium" AI features.

Winning the title in the category of air hammers, the M18 Fuel Striker Hammer Chisel Kit is integrated with a Powerstate motor that can deliver a striking force of up to 7 joules to help separate old and rusty components when performing automotive repairs, such as suspension teardowns, ball joint removals, wheel pin removal, and more. Basically, the tool delivers repeated hammering force using a chisel attachment at one of three speeds, with a maximum of 3,000 BPM.

The RedLink Plus Intelligence technology featured in this hammer gun protects it against overload, overheating, and over-discharge, while there's also an LED light added at the base of the design for workspace illumination. Moreover, it has a .401-inch round-shank twist chuck, which securely connects the attachment to the tool without requiring additional tools.

The Pro Tool Innovation Awards described this Milwaukee power tool as "literally the world's first cordless air hammer specifically designed for automotive applications." The M12 Fuel 1/4″ Extended Die Grinder is the winner in the Cordless Die Grinder category at the awards. It is a multi-purpose tool that can grind, polish, and cut, as well as remove old or unwanted paint, rust, and other material from metal surfaces. Powered by a Powerstate motor, it can generate up to 20,000 RPM, though you can pick one of the four speed ranges. The 4-inch shaft design helps the tool work in confined spaces, while a 1/4-inch collet makes it compatible with a range of accessories.

There's also a push-button spindle lock that keeps the tool locked while performing accessory changes using a simple wrench. The cordless power tool can fit a 2-inch cutting wheel and 3-inch sanding accessories. Also, it comes with a built-in LED light to keep the work area well-lit. Built with the ability to produce up to 2,000 foot-pounds of nut-busting torque, it can remove old and stubborn lugs and bolts from vehicles and machinery. Meanwhile, the peak fastening torque goes up to 1,800 foot-pounds to tackle large fasteners.

In addition, it features a four-mode control system that lets you control the speed and power of the tool to match the job's demands. In mode four, it automatically reduces torque to 75 foot-pounds in forward mode to prevent overtightening; in reverse, it slows down once the fastener is loose for controlled removal.

According to Milwaukee, since it is part of the M18 line of tools, pairing it with an M18 RedLithium Forge XC8.0 battery can enable the tool gun to install up to 120 1-1/4-inch bolts on a single charge. A heavy-duty cordless saw kit designed for professionals who need to cut through thick pieces of wood and lumber on the jobsite, the M18 Fuel 10-1/4″ Rear Handle Circular Saw Kit delivers the power they need.
