#394. Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further.
  • In a recent development, TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i.
  • Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the firm announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.

In a recent development, TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.

Sampling, serving and reasoning.

Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training.

Two TPU 8i chips on one package.

It has been revealed that for the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.

Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.

According to recent reports, the memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.

Recent findings suggest that google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The organization has also declared the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.

It has been revealed that google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One glitch with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the latest generation differs.

It has been revealed that in contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the upcoming TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.

According to recent reports, this chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.

It has been revealed that google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.

The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.

It has been revealed that the 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.

In a recent development, what is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are at the moment listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.

Delivering two newly introduced TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.

#393. 'Sharp and futuristic': I rode Honda's first full-sized electric motorcycle

'Sharp and futuristic': I rode Honda's first full-sized electric motorcycle

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Up until this point, the electric motorcycle industry has been largely dominated by a brace of brave startups, keen on proving that battery packs and electric motors make the perfect powertrain for a two-wheeler.
  • Maeving has been plowing ahead with its retro-inspired range of excellent city bikes, while Zero has been refining its line of adventure and performance machines for more than 20 years.
  • Harley-Davidson bucked the trend and was arguably the first major-name brand to put its reputation on the line, but sales haven’t exactly been going swimmingly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Up until this point, the electric motorcycle industry has been largely dominated by a brace of brave startups, keen on proving that battery packs and electric motors make the perfect powertrain for a two-wheeler.

Maeving has been plowing ahead with its retro-inspired range of excellent city bikes, while Zero has been refining its line of adventure and performance machines for more than 20 years.

Harley-Davidson bucked the trend and was arguably the first major-name brand to put its reputation on the line, but sales haven’t exactly been going swimmingly.

There are more names to mention, but the sector hasn't yet experienced anywhere near the sort of sales figures that electrified passenger vehicles have. Perhaps it is crying out for a more recognizable brand to get involved?

Now in steps Honda… one of the world’s most recognized automotive brands. After impressing with its CUV e electric scooter, it has decided to take things to the next level and release its first series-production, full-size electric motorcycle in the WN7. This could be just what the market needed.

Recent findings suggest that let’s deal with the name first, because it is, by far, one of the worst things about this machine. The ‘W’ apparently stands for ‘Wind,’ while the ‘N’ represents ‘Naked,’ as in it doesn’t have a fairing.

The seven? Well, that’s an indication of where it sits in the lineup, a bit like Kia’s EV naming strategy.

As is the way with many electric motorcycles, the WN7 can be specified in two power outputs: an 11kW A1-license-friendly version and an altogether more powerful 18kW version for those with a full A2 license.

Of course, licensing regulations differ throughout the world (apologies if you’re reading this from the US), but you get the idea. It can be purchased and ridden by people with a range of experience levels.

Even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration.

But the quirk of electric motorcycling is that both models have a peak power output of 50kW, or around 67bhp, and a hefty 100Nm of torque.

In other words, even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration.

In a recent development, the 9.3kWh lithium-ion battery is a 'stressed member', so the big block at the front essentially acts as part of the chassis. For this reason, the batteries aren’t removable, but it looks cool and makes the WN7 handle like a real sport bike.

In typical electric motorcycle fashion, there’s no clutch or gear lever to contend with. It’s just a case of twisting the throttle and hanging on.

The brakes, thankfully, are laid out like those on a traditional combustion motorcycle, with a lever mounted on the handlebar and a pedal by the right foot that controls the rear brake.

There’s a ‘tank,’ but it’s not filled with fuel. Instead, it houses the charging port, which can handle low-speed home charging as well as DC fast charging at public stations.

Honda states that using one of these, a 20% to 80% charge takes around 30 minutes. That’s enough for another 50 miles of riding in the time it takes to stretch the legs and an improvement on what Zero Motorcycles right now offers — although DC fast charging is promised for 2027.

Overall, Honda's claimed maximum range is 87 miles on a single charge, but, as you’ll see later, this is a tad unrealistic.

Sources indicate that firing up the WN7 is an interesting process. A remote key fob stays in your pocket, while a small ignition button on the frame turns everything on. From there, you pull in the brake lever, press a thumb switch on the handlebar, and it’s ready to go.

Recent findings suggest that cleverly, Honda has added forward and reverse assist, so it’s much easier to maneuver the 217kg machine at low speeds. Holding one of the corresponding buttons and gently twisting the throttle moves the bike backward or forward.

As you would expect from a Honda, everything immediately feels solid and well-built.

As you would expect from a Honda, everything immediately feels solid and well-built, while the decision to specify things like Showa inverted forks and large disc brakes with two-piston calipers up front inspires confidence.

The low center of gravity, aided by a whopping battery mounted low in the frame, makes it feel super stable, even at slow speeds.

Plus, the adjustable regenerative braking, accessed via paddles on the handlebar, makes it easy to set the amount of ‘engine braking’ the bike delivers.

This is important, because there’s nothing weirder than rolling off the throttle only for an electric motorcycle to coast almost forever. Adding a touch of regenerative braking means the bike slows as you ease off the throttle, which will feel far more natural for anyone used to combustion bikes.

Performance is strong and, like many larger electric motorcycles I have tested, the acceleration is almost sickeningly quick.

It has been revealed that A lack of gears makes the 0–60mph dash feel like being fired out of a cannon. Just pure torque and acceleration, before the WN7 runs out of puff at around 70mph.

According to recent reports, the bike is limited to 80mph, so it’s great for overtaking on slower country roads, but I found it a bit disconcerting when traffic started moving promptly. On highways, for example, where traffic flows at a steady 75mph, the WN7 feels underpowered.

But, perhaps more importantly, this feels like a proper Honda product. Much like the CUV e-scooter, the Japanese marque has put its stamp on a category that sometimes lacks finesse.

Aside from the uncomfortable seat, which looks like it has taken its color palette from a dentist’s chair, and the charging port, which likes to ping open with the mildest of touches, there’s a lot to like about the WN7 stylistically.

Industry observers note that it’s sharp, futuristic, and looks like very little else in the current Honda lineup. The massive TFT dash is ultra-bright and controlled via simple switchgear on the handlebar, although Honda has missed a trick by not adding true smartphone mirroring.

Instead, there’s a Honda RoadSync smartphone app that connects via Bluetooth and offers very simple navigation on the display, as well as music controls and some EV telemetry.

But pull over at an EV charging station and you’ll be accosted by bikers and electric car drivers alike. It’s a proper head-turner and conversation starter.

Get used to it, because you’ll be stopping at charging stations a lot (unless you tuck it away in a garage and sensibly charge overnight). The range is still just as much of an concern as it is with Honda’s rivals.

Industry observers note that the advertised 87 miles might be realistic if you simply use the bike for a quick dash across town, but the bike slurps juice like a thirsty Fortnite character anywhere else. During an admittedly very cold loan period, I watched the range drop in front of my eyes while enjoying the 60mph forest roads nearby.

During one day spent with it, when I captured the images for this feature, I probably covered around 50 miles on a full charge and managed to limp home with 5% battery remaining.

It feels cruel to get all this way and not mention the price. At £12,999 in the UK (around $17,200 / AU$25,300), the WN7 might be more expensive than similarly powerful Honda combustion bikes, but it’s very competitive compared to its electric rivals.

The Can-Am Pulse and LiveWire S2 are arguably its closest challengers, but Honda manages to hold its own with a mature ride, excellent build quality, and the all-crucial fast-charging technology.

Despite this, I couldn’t help coming away from my time with the bike wishing Honda — an engineering juggernaut — had done more.

According to recent reports, the WN7 still feels heavy, the range remains an glitch, and it’s not exactly shout-from-the-rooftops exciting to ride. There are just so many unforgettably visceral petrol bikes out there at this price.

But this feels like just the start, and if Honda gets cooking, we’re guaranteed to see an electric motorcycle that can finally hold its own against the combustion competition in the very near future.

With its generous 3D cache, it's one of the very best gaming CPUs on the market right now, edged out only by the 9850X3D in terms of gaming performance, as you can see from our bench database below. With 8 cores and 16 threads, this CPU will chew through any gaming title thanks to that 3D cache, which means the chip has to rely much less heavily on RAM, drastically improving performance.

The GPU in this build is the RX 9070 with a generous 16GB of VRAM. Sadly, it isn't the more potent XT version, but this is still a great gaming GPU, averaging nearly 75 FPS in our 19-game rasterization benchmark suite at 1440p. 4K performance was around 41 FPS without frame generation, too, so there is some 4K potential.

According to recent reports, the PC also comes with 32GB of DDR5 5600 memory, a slight compromise over 6000 speeds but one you shouldn't notice too much. You also get a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD for your operating system and storing games, plenty to get you started.

Recent findings suggest that it's all held together by a B650 motherboard, and ships inside one of CyberPower's more impressive cases, along with fans aplenty. You also get Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, lots of USB ports, HDMI and DisplayPort connectivity, and a liquid cooler for the CPU, as well as an 850-watt power supply. And, of course, a copy of Windows 11.

With Black Friday still a couple of weeks away, this is one of the best gaming PC deals going right now and one not to be missed.

Alice Huang, the person allegedly involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly surfaced in Beijing, marking the first sighting of the Megaspeed executive since the scandal broke out. According to Bloomberg, it’s unclear when the suspected Chinese spy arrived in the capital or why she’s in the area, but she was last spotted leaving Singapore for Shanghai in 2025 after she was detained and questioned during the city-state’s investigation into the $2-billion smuggling case involving Megaspeed.

The Nvidia CEO is now under intense scrutiny after the revelation of his indiscretion with the Megaspeed executive, with Congress threatening to problem a subpoena if he does not respond to their invitation to “a joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. The FBI is also looking into the relationship between the head of the largest AI hardware organization in the world and a person suspected of helping sanctioned Chinese companies secure hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips. Overnight, a second bombshell report claims that Jensen Huang was also involved in an extramarital affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.

Recent findings suggest that although the Chinese embassy in Washington has denied any links to Alice Huang, calling it nothing but “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing, there is speculation that she’s under the control of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is the primary agency that handles China’s foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. The U.S. intelligence community suggests that she may be passing on information to the MSS, but it remains unclear if she was specifically tasked by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang or if they were only leveraging her relationship with the Nvidia chief to get insights into the U.S. AI industry.

A deeper investigation into Alice Huang, known by her Chinese name as Huang Le, revealed that she supposedly worked in media before jumping into banking and finance. The Wall Street Journal reports that it’s unclear when she met her husband, Kang Wei, but the couple ran a private equity and investment management firm called Shanghai Hexi in 2016. This allowed the couple to invest in companies across industries, including gaming, pharmaceuticals, and, eventually, data centers and cloud computing.

According to recent reports, the couple is known for riding trends and isn’t a stranger to scandals. Their firm, Shanghai Hexi, invested in gaming companies in the 2010s, especially when mobile gaming started to boom across the world, while Chinese regulators fined Kang and the organization in 2018 for disclosure failures and other violations while it was in the midst of a takeover battle for a corporation. Kang’s moves in the gaming industry are what allowed him to meet Jensen Huang, which eventually led to a close relationship between the couple and the Nvidia chief. Sources told the WSJ that Kang apparently accepted Alice and Jensen’s extra-marital relationship, even sometimes jokingly telling people that she was Jensen’s “personal assistant.”.

It has been revealed that it seems that the couple is used to leveraging their relationships to gain business advantage, and with investments in AI data centers expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, Alice Huang’s “close” relationship with Jensen Huang put Shanghai Hexi in an excellent position to take advantage of the trend through Megaspeed and make big money. And with U.S. sanctions making it harder for competitors to acquire Nvidia chips, it appears that their access has turned into a gold mine for the organization. But whether Alice Huang acted solely out of business interest with the supposed procurement of Nvidia chips or was leveraged by Chinese authorities to import these chips, the fact remains that $7.5 billion worth of banned chips reportedly made their way into China despite Washington’s efforts.

In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a big homepage redesign that has three core components.

Upgrade 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s presently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

Sources indicate that you’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside upcoming chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.

These updates are at the moment in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some customers have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Online design tool Canva has just debuted Canva Craft, its first AI image generation model that lets you make all sorts of visual content to add to the things you create.
  • Sources indicate that if you already rely on ChatGPT or another AI tool to create visuals for you but you also regularly use Canva, it could be a good way to combine image generation and design in one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online design tool Canva has just debuted Canva Craft, its first AI image generation model that lets you make all sorts of visual content to add to the things you create. So think social media and marketing materials, lifestyle photography, digital art, characters, nature imagery and more.

Sources indicate that if you already rely on ChatGPT or another AI tool to create visuals for you but you also regularly use Canva, it could be a good way to combine image generation and design in one. And although it may not be as powerful as ChatGPT, it might not be far off. Canva notes its in-house AI lab, Canva Research, is “the world’s second most advanced lab for image generation” behind OpenAI.

Industry observers note that I wanted to find out exactly how Canva’s upcoming AI image generation capabilities compare to ChatGPT’s, so I put the free version of Canva and the free version of ChatGPT head-to-head with five image tests. I gave each tool prompts that were aligned with some of the examples Canva gave in its announcement, like making product photography or blog imagery, and the results are below.

In a recent development, every time Canva creates an image, it presents five options. I chose the first one to make the test fair and presented that on the left of every picture here. With ChatGPT, it tends to make one image, though several times in this test it presented two side-by-side and asked me to pick my favorite to perfect the model. Again, I always went with the first and presented that on the right of every picture below.

In a recent development, if you want to know how each AI image generation tool compares, this should be a good starting point for working out which produces the best results and which might be the best option for you. For each prompt I chose a winner based on personal preference, taking into account whether it looked realistic, fit the prompt and whether I could imagine using it in actual design projects.

Prompt: Create a polished product photo of a premium silver flip phone on a stone pedestal, with soft studio lighting and a clean beige background.

In a recent development, I know some people who use Canva for design mock-ups, especially for ads, websites and social media assets. Which is why I wanted to see how Canva and ChatGPT compare when it comes to creating a realistic-looking product photography.

Sources indicate that both Canva and ChatGPT nailed the brief with a very similar interpretation of the prompt. The lighting and textures are certainly believable and have all the hallmarks of a product photoshoot.

Of course, if you wanted to use them for a particular product, you’d have to get very specific with the prompt because in these examples these phones clearly don’t exist.

Prompt: Create a realistic flat lay of a laptop, notebook, coffee cup, phone, pen and glasses neatly arranged on a wooden desk.

I often see people sharing pictures of their desk to add to a LinkedIn post or blog post about the way they work or creativity. A birds eye view of a desk is also a pretty standard image for websites. So I thought this would be a handy test and give us an opportunity to assess the textures and physics of the AI images.

Sources indicate that both of the results here looked believable enough to add to a simple blog or social media post. But zoom in and there are some differences. Mostly that the Canva version looks a little less realistic in my opinion due to the angle of the objects and the textures, especially in the coffee.

The lighting is a lot more interesting in the Canva version, though the artificial-looking lighting in the ChatGPT image actually makes the scene look more believably office-like.

Prompt: Create a realistic photo of a woman laughing outside a café on a sunny morning, with natural light and a candid editorial feel.

Recent findings suggest that I intentionally kept this prompt loose to see how both AI tools would run with it. At first, the interpretations looked similar, same sort of café in the background, same sunny lighting and same expression.

Recent findings suggest that but it didn’t take me long to see that Canva’s version was much more basic. The image it created could maybe work in a blog post at a push, but not if anyone zoomed in. The skin was overly smooth and there were some consistency problems with the woman’s mouth, which didn’t quite line up properly at the edges. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t great.

In a recent development, in comparison, ChatGPT created a woman who looked much more realistic. Her skin had texture, her expression was more natural, she looked like a regular woman rather than overly made up and I couldn’t spot any inconsistencies no matter how hard I searched for them.

Prompt: Design a modern poster for an art exhibition called “The Art of Disconnecting” with bold typography, a clean layout and an image of a flip phone.

Recent findings suggest that canva already provides intuitive and granular ways to make posters. I don’t think the point of Canva Craft is to bypass that. But at the same time, I know people are using AI more and more now to whip up really quick posters and flyers, so I wanted to compare them.

Both nailed text rendering, which is expected nowadays but still good to see. It doesn’t feel like that long ago when ChatGPT was pumping out posters with nonsensical letters.

In a recent development, both also picked a similar color palette and design for this prompt, which was interesting. It makes it hard to judge them as the general aesthetic is almost identical.

The Canva version added more opportunities to put details onto the poster, which is maybe more practical but made the result look a bit busy. For this reason, the ChatGPT version was a little more impactful for me. But it was close.

Prompt: Create a dream-like image of a flip phone opening into a childhood bedroom, with a nostalgic, surreal and slightly melancholic mood.

It has been revealed that I know some people use Canva to make blog post graphics they can’t find elsewhere, so I wanted to try something a little more abstract for this final prompt. I recently wrote a newsletter about how my old phones sometimes appear in my dreams and wondered how the two tools would interpret that nostalgic and surreal sort of vibe.

It was interesting to see how they changed the tone to accommodate the dream-like prompt. In all honesty, I didn’t particularly like either and wouldn’t have used them.

But I think the Canva one was marginally better, with clearer imagery that followed the brief more than ChatGPT’s super surreal and squashed-looking effort.

I preferred ChatGPT’s image generation, but I was surprised at how close Canva came and how realistic-looking its results were. The big question, however, is how both tools compare on price and usage. This is where ChatGPT makes much more sense for most people, but it really depends on the plan you use.

With Canva, all users have a monthly AI allowance. If you’re on the free plan that’s really small and you can expect to max out your allowance in five prompts. Now, that is because for every results you’ll get four options. So technically speaking you can generate 20 images a month. But that’s still not many.

In a recent development, if you pay for Canva, the amount of images you can make will depend on your specific AI allowance. With Canva Pro ($18 / £13 / AU$20 per month) you’ll get roughly 200 per month. That goes up to about 400 on the Business initiative ($25 / £18 / AU$28 per month).

Recent findings suggest that with ChatGPT's free version, it can depend from user to user. But you can usually create about five images per day. So that’s a lot more than Canva’s free tool, which only gives you that a month.

Sources indicate that with ChatGPT Plus ($20 / £19.99 / AU$29.99 per month), again it depends as there are no official limits. But it’s not unlimited, so you can expect to make hundreds of images every few hours.

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, austrian cooling outfit Noctua is officially rolling its new NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM4 and AM5 processors into the retail market.
  • Conventional thermal pastes and most thermal pads gradually lose performance over time due to pump-out, delamination, cracking, and other forms of degradation.
  • This allows heat transfer performance to improve during the initial activation period rather than gradually deteriorating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, austrian cooling outfit Noctua is officially rolling its new NT-CP1 AM5/4 Carbice carbon nanotube thermal pad for AMD AM4 and AM5 processors into the retail market. After announcing its partnership with advanced nanotechnology tech giant Carbice back in June 2026, the premium thermal pad can now be purchased for $24.95 in the US and €24.95 in the European region.

Conventional thermal pastes and most thermal pads gradually lose performance over time due to pump-out, delamination, cracking, and other forms of degradation. However, Noctua says that its new NT-CP1 thermal pad takes a different approach. It makes use of Carbice's vertically-aligned carbon nanotube technology, originally developed for high thermal reliability in aerospace systems. The carbon nanotubes gradually conform to microscopic imperfections of a CPU’s IHS over hundreds to thousands of thermal cycles.

This allows heat transfer performance to improve during the initial activation period rather than gradually deteriorating. The thermal pad can also maintain stable, maintenance-free performance for years once the initial activation phase is complete. Thus, making it a suitable option for people who want consistent thermal performance without having to periodically replace degraded thermal paste.

"Carbice pads offer a unique combination of ultimate performance stability and convenient installation. This makes the NT-CP1 the perfect choice for everyone who’s looking for a thermal pad that’s super easy to apply and never needs to be replaced," said Noctua CEO Roland Mossig in a press note.

Unlike conventional carbon or graphite-based thermal pads, which can be brittle, slippery, and electrically conductive, the NT-CP1 features an aluminum backbone sandwiched between layers of carbon nanotubes. The surface is also protected by a nanoscale polymer coating, which Noctua claims makes the pad more robust, easier to handle, and less likely to move during installation. The firm recommends a simple peel, press, and peel installation process, while the slightly tacky coating helps keep the pad in place and offers electrical insulation as long as the polymer layer remains intact.

With an ultra-thin 90µm profile and precut 33x33mm size, the thermal pad fits both AM5 and AM4 socket processors. Noctua also highlights its manufacturing process, noting that the pad is produced in the US using recycled aluminum and waste carbon gas to grow the carbon nanotubes. The company claims that its manufacturing process is more energy-efficient compared to conventional graphite and graphene-based pads, while the aluminum structure allows the product to be recycled through standard aluminum recycling channels.

Samsung has finally declared Galaxy Sync for Galaxy smartphones, allowing people to automatically sync photos and videos from Samsung Gallery to Google Photos in the background.

Industry observers note that after Samsung ended its partnership with Microsoft OneDrive earlier this year, there were reports that the company would partner with Google to bring a new Gallery Sync feature to Galaxy smartphones, allowing consumers to sync their photos directly from Samsung Gallery to Google Photos. And now, the feature is finally here.

According to Samsung's official announcement, the latest Gallery Sync feature allows customers to back up their photos and videos directly to Google's cloud storage without having to switch to another app. All you need to do is sign in with your Samsung and Google accounts and enable the feature in the Gallery app.

What's interesting is that the upcoming integration also makes it easier to access your photos across multiple Galaxy devices.

For example, if you take a photo on your Galaxy smartphone, you'll be able to see it in the Gallery app on your Galaxy tablet, provided both devices are signed in with the same accounts and have syncing enabled.

Samsung is also introducing a new "Free up space on this phone" feature that lets customers remove photos and videos from their device once they've been backed up to Google storage. The Gallery app will continue showing thumbnails of those files, and you can download the original versions whenever you need them.

In a recent development, as for storage, the feature uses your existing Google account storage, which is shared across Google Photos, Gmail, and Google Drive. This means you get the same 15GB of free storage that comes with a Google account.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

It has been revealed that there is, however, one limitation worth keeping in mind. The newly introduced integration doesn't mean your entire Google Photos library will automatically appear in Samsung Gallery. For now, only photos and videos synced through Samsung Gallery after enabling the feature will show up across your supported Galaxy devices.

In terms of compatibility, Galaxy Sync has started rolling out to Galaxy devices running One UI 9, and Samsung says it will expand availability to more devices in phases.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The fresh Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be substantial-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

It has been revealed that meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a major reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the tech giant’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest substantial change, as the firm moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s board of directors has confirmed today that Jensen Huang has resigned as the tech giant's CEO. The news follows revelations that Huang had been involved in not one but two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and another with his direct report, Nvidia’s VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.

"NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," the board stated. "Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.".

According to recent reports, in recent weeks, stories have come to light alleging that Huang was involved in an overly familiar relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect may be a Chinese intelligence asset. It was reported that the AI GPU giant’s CEO may have been the target of a spy plot — Megaspeed is under investigation for its involvement in the smuggling of $2 billion worth of export-controlled AI GPUs into China.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 10 percent in early market trading following the news, and are now down more than 23% in the last month.

Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife and issued a company-wide apology. Separately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors debuted an independent investigation into reports that Huang’s entanglement may be a matter of national security, given his role in the global AI revolution.

Colette Kress has been Nvidia's Executive Vice President and CFO since September 2013; prior to that, she spent 25 years at Cisco and Microsoft, among others.

Industry observers note that just a couple of days later, a second bombshell report emerged claiming that Jensen Huang was also romantically involved with Powell, one of his direct reports at the company. Reports indicate the affair was known within the company, and that the two were even filmed being affectionate in a San Jose hotel at Nvidia GTC. Security allegedly sequestered a bystander who filmed the interaction on camera and made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Google has announced the November Pixel Drop for Pixel phones, bringing a massive list of newly introduced features to both newer and older Pixel smartphones.

Recent findings suggest that google releases Pixel Drops every few months, bringing fresh features and improvements to its Pixel devices beyond the usual security patches and bug fixes. While some of these updates are relatively minor, the latest November Pixel Drop is a pretty substantial one, especially if you're using a Pixel 10 series smartphone.

That's because Google is bringing several features that were previously exclusive to the Pixel 11 series to last year's flagships.

According to Google's official announcement, the November Pixel Drop brings Gemini Intelligence to the Pixel 10 series, including features like Rambler, Gemini's ability to handle multi-step tasks, and personalized suggestions.

For example, if someone sends you a text asking about your ETA while you're already using Google Maps, your Pixel can provide timely suggestions and actions based on what you're doing.

Another interesting addition is Create My Widget, which lets customers create home screen widgets with natural language prompts. Instead of relying on existing widgets, you can simply describe what you want, and Google will generate one for you.

The feature is available on the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series, although the Pixel 10a is notably missing from the list.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In a recent development, google has also introduced new custom icon styles with the November Pixel Drop. The company has added 10 different styles to choose from, which use its Nano Banana AI model to generate matching app icons and give your home screen a more consistent look.

Recent findings suggest that beyond customization, Google is bringing its Pixel Search experience to older devices, allowing users to search across apps, messages, photos, emails, and device settings directly from their phones. The feature is now available on the Pixel 6 series and newer devices.

According to recent reports, google hasn't forgotten about its latest phones either, and there are a couple of features exclusive to the Pixel 11 series. Google is upgrading Call Screen with Gemini, allowing the AI assistant to have more natural conversations with unknown callers while showing a live transcript on your phone.

There are upgrades to the HiLight feature on the Pixel 11 Pro phones as well, which can now light up when you receive a Google Messages notification. Unfortunately, there's still no support for third-party messaging apps like WhatsApp or Telegram.

In addition to the Pixel Drop, Google has also announced the availability of the Pixel Tag, which it first unveiled alongside the Pixel 11 series in August. The tracker is now available individually for $29.99 or as a four-pack for $99.99. It uses Google's upgraded Find Hub network and supports ultra-wideband (UWB) for precision tracking.

Sources indicate that as for availability, Google states the November Pixel Drop started rolling out on November 10 and will continue reaching supported devices over the next several weeks. We haven't received the OTA patch on our Pixel 11 Pro just yet, but considering Google's usual rollout schedule, you should hopefully see it arrive on your device within the next few days.

#369. Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic

Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that built by CWT, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a showpiece that backs its looks with real substance.
  • It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • In a recent development, corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that built by CWT, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a showpiece that backs its looks with real substance. Efficiency is excellent, regulation and ripple are tight, and the fanless window covers half of its rated output at room temperature. Taiwanese capacitors, a noisy hot run and a 200 mm long chassis are the compromises, while the ten-year warranty and iCUE LINK integration add genuine value.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In a recent development, corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades. Founded in California in 1994 as a manufacturer of memory modules, the company has since grown into one of the largest brands in the PC component and peripheral market, with a catalog that covers cases, cooling, keyboards, mice, streaming gear, and of course, power supplies. Corsair entered the PSU market in the second half of the 2000s and built its reputation there by choosing its OEM partners carefully rather than manufacturing in-house. Channel Well Technology (CWT) has been one of the most important of these partners, producing a large portion of the RMx and HXi units over the years. The HXi series in particular has long been Corsair's high-end, digitally monitored family, positioned just below the flagship AX models.

Industry observers note that we take a closer look at the HX1000i Shift Crystal to see if it deserves a spot in our best power supplies list. The HX1000i Shift Crystal is a bit of an odd bird, and Corsair is clearly fine with that. First shown at Computex 2026 and launching on November 12th, it combines the side-mounted connector layout of the SHIFT models with the digital HXi platform, and then wraps everything in a chassis with clear polycarbonate panels on three sides, turning the internals of the PSU into a part of the build's aesthetics. Beneath the show, the platform is built by CWT. It holds a Cybenetics Platinum certification at both 115 VAC and 230 VAC, and it is fully compliant with the ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 design guides. It also integrates an iCUE LINK System Hub and Corsair's PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring for the native 12V-2x6 connector. The 1000W model that we are reviewing today is rated to deliver its full power output continuously at ambient temperatures up to 50°C and comes with a ten-year warranty.

Sources indicate that the HX1000i Shift Crystal ships in a very large and sturdy black cardboard box, with a large render of the unit on the front that does a good job of showing off the transparent panels and the lit fan. The model name is printed in substantial yellow and white letters across the bottom half, while the badges in the top right corner - ATX 3.1 with PCIe 5.1 and 12V-2x6 support, the Cybenetics certifications, and the iCUE LINK logo- tell you most of what you need to know before even opening the package.

Industry observers note that the bundle is rather spartan for a product of this class. Inside the box, we found the AC power cord, four mounting screws, a handful of black cable ties, and a leaflet with safety and compliance information. There are no Velcro straps, no cable combs beyond those already on the cables, and no other accessories of any kind. It is not a deal breaker by any means, but a premium unit like this that is focused on aesthetics could have been a little more generous in this department.

According to recent reports, all of the cables are fully modular and black, with individually sleeved wires and low-profile cable combs. There is a 24-pin ATX cable, two 4+4-pin EPS cables, three PCIe cables carrying four 6+2-pin connectors in total, and a native 12V-2x6 cable rated for 600W, alongside two SATA and two Molex cables with four connectors each. Eight Molex connectors on a modern 1000W unit is extremely generous, frankly more than any reasonable build will ever need. Corsair also supplies two iCUE LINK cables of different lengths and a USB cable that connects the PSU's monitoring interface to the motherboard.

Recent findings suggest that with dimensions of 150 x 86 x 200 mm, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a long ATX unit, which is a non-issue if you are getting the matching Corsair 4500X case anyway. In any other case, you will need to check your case's specifications before buying one. The side-mounted SHIFT connectors also require some free space next to the PSU, as the cables plug into the side of the unit instead of its face, which is great for cases with a hidden PSU compartment but not suitable for every chassis. The design is unlike anything else on the market. The steel frame is black, with Y-shaped cutouts forming the fan grille and a debossed pattern of the same shape on the opposite panel, while three of the sides are clear polycarbonate panels that reveal the white fan frame, the bulk capacitors, the coils, and the white PCBs. With the RGB fan lit, the unit very much looks like a piece of display hardware rather than a power supply.

In a recent development, the rear of the unit is a little more conventional, with the AC receptacle, a rocker on/off switch marked with the "HX1000i SHIFT" logo, and a large perforated area with the same Y-shaped cutouts for the exhaust. The modular connector bay is on the side, behind the clear panel. The face opposite the AC receptacle hosts the white control PCB, also visible through its clear panel, with two iCUE LINK ports, a USB Type-C port, and a small port marked "TACH". The hexagonal specifications sticker is on the solid steel top side of the unit and is an envelope-type that can be closed to hide the text.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The CRYSTAL is fully compatible with Corsair's iCUE software, which can be used to monitor the PSU, adjust its fan speed, and switch the 12V overcurrent protection between single- and multi-rail modes. Corsair also integrated an iCUE LINK System Hub that, according to the company, supports up to 24 iCUE LINK devices without the need for a separate hub. The most interesting addition, however, is PinProtect+, Corsair's per-pin current monitoring for the 12V-2x6 connector. If the current on a pin exceeds a user-customizable threshold, the PSU cuts power to the connector, and the RGB fan lighting turns red to signal the fault. Given the history of melting connectors, this is a genuinely useful feature rather than marketing fluff. We can confirm that it is working as intended, as we tried pulling 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector and the PSU shut down instantly.

Cooling is handled by a 140 mm Corsair NR140HL-RGB fan. Corsair calls it a magnetic dome bearing design, and in practice it is a rifle-bearing fan with a half-domed shaft magnet, rated at 0.55A on 12V. The fan is white with addressable lighting, which also doubles as the visual alarm for PinProtect+. It is a decent fan, and the magnetic shaft should help with longevity, but it is worth mentioning that the regular HX1000i SHIFT uses a fluid dynamic bearing fan, which we would normally consider the better choice for a premium unit.

Industry observers note that the OEM behind the HX1000i Shift Crystal is Channel Well Technology (CWT), Corsair's long-time partner for its HXi units. Almost every part inside the unit has been relabeled as "Corsair", including the capacitors and the magnetic components, so the OEM is not obvious at a glance, but the Cybenetics report confirms it. The layout is extremely clean and obviously optimized for aesthetics, which also explains the excessive length of the chassis. The bridge rectifiers have their own heatsink, the APFC components sit on another large heatsink, and the primary switchers have their own heatsink as well, while the secondary side components are on a vertical PCB right after the main transformer. All heatsinks are of good size and quality.

The transient filtering stage has four Y capacitors, three X capacitors, and two filtering inductors. Two bridge rectifiers sharing a large heatsink feed the APFC stage, which relies on two Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs and two fully encased filtering coils. The APFC stage also includes two bulk capacitors, one Corsair 560 μF / 420 V capacitor and one Corsair 470 μF / 420 V capacitor, for a combined capacity of 1030 μF. According to the Cybenetics report, these capacitors are supplied by Elite, a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, and they are rated for 105°C. They are not capacitors that we frequently encounter in anything above mid-tier, though, and we feel they are not a great match for a premium unit.

Sources indicate that the primary inversion stage uses two more Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs in a half-bridge LLC resonant topology. On the secondary side, ten Infineon 014N04LS MOSFETs handle the synchronous rectification of the 12V rail, and the minor rails are derived from DC-to-DC converters. All of the capacitors on the secondary side are rebranded as Corsair, with black and white sleeves that match the color scheme of the unit, and are also made by Elite. These are mostly good parts, but it is a bit ironic that Corsair advertises 105°C Japanese electrolytic capacitors for the regular HX1000i SHIFT, while the version built to show its capacitors off uses Taiwanese ones.

For the testing of PSUs, we are using high-precision electronic loads with a maximum power draw of 2700 Watts, a Rigol DS5042M 40 MHz oscilloscope, an Extech 380803 power analyzer, two high-precision UNI-T UT-325 digital thermometers, an Extech HD600 SPL meter, a self-designed hotbox, and various other bits and parts.

According to recent reports, at 25°C ambient, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a very efficient power supply. It averaged 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC across the nominal load range, with the efficiency peaking at 93.6% (230 VAC) and 92.2% (115 VAC) at around 40% load. The curve is relatively flat after that, with the unit still achieving 91% at 230 VAC and 88.5% at 115 VAC while delivering its full 1000W. The efficiency at very low loads is good as well, at just over 88% with a 50W load on 230 VAC. These figures are in line with the unit's Cybenetics Platinum certification at both input voltages. There is no 80 PLUS certification for this unit.

The acoustics at room temperature are very good. The fan stays completely off up to 50% load, so a typical gaming system with a powerful graphics card will rarely ever wake it up. Once it starts, the unit registers 31.6 dB(A) at 500W, and the fan ramps up very gently, staying around 33 dB(A) at 700W and below 37 dB(A) at 900W. Only at full load does the noise climb to about 39 dB(A), which is still a low figure for a 1000W unit. Thermal performance gives no reason for concern at all, with the primary and secondary heatsinks reaching just 55°C and 58°C respectively at full load.

Inside our hotbox, at roughly 45°C ambient and still within the unit's 50°C rating, the HX1000i Shift Crystal hardly lost any efficiency at all. It averaged 91.7% at 230 VAC and 90.1% at 115 VAC, a drop of just 0.4 percentage points compared to the cold test. The peak efficiency dropped to 93.3% and 91.9%, respectively, and the full-load efficiency to 90.6% and 88.1%. That is a very strong result that shows how well the platform tolerates high ambient temperatures.

The fan is the part that changes its behavior the most in the heat. It starts spinning a bit earlier, at about 400W, registering 32.2 dB(A), and the noise climbs relatively fast to about 36 dB(A) at 600W and 39.5 dB(A) at 700W. Beyond 800W, the fan profile becomes much more aggressive, with the unit reaching 45.7 dB(A) at 900W and 46.8 dB(A) at its maximum output. That is definitely loud, though it takes very adverse conditions to get there. Internal temperatures rose considerably, with the primary heatsink reaching 84°C and the secondary heatsink 89°C at full load, figures that are high but comfortably within what the platform can handle.

Sources indicate that voltage regulation is very good. Across the 20% to 100% load range, the 12V rail deviated by 1%, from 12.10V down to 11.98V; the 5V rail by 1% as well; and the 3.3V rail by just 0.7%. These are not the sub-0.5% figures of the very best digital platforms on the market, but all of the rails are well controlled, and the 12V rail stays very close to its nominal voltage across the whole load range. The ripple suppression is excellent. The 12V rail peaked at 48 mV under maximum load and 44 mV during the 12V cross-load test, while the 5V and 3.3V rails both topped out at 26 mV. Compared to the ATX design limits of 120 mV and 50 mV, that leaves a margin of 60% on the 12V rail and about 48% on the minor rails, which is very comfortable headroom for a 1000W unit.

During our thorough assessment, we evaluate the essential protection features of every power supply unit we review, including Over Current Protection (OCP), Over Voltage Protection (OVP), Over Power Protection (OPP), and Short Circuit Protection (SCP).

All protection mechanisms were verified and triggered correctly during testing. With the unit hot, OCP tripped at 148% (37A) on the 3.3V rail, 144% (36A) on the 5V rail, and 132% (110A) on the 12V rail, with OPP shutting the unit down at 130% of its rated output, or 1300W. These thresholds are on the high side, especially for the minor rails, but they are not unusual for an ATX 3.1 unit.

In a recent development, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a power supply designed to be looked at, and that is not something we often get to say. Corsair took a CWT-built HXi platform, cleaned up its layout to the point that it can be shown off, and placed it behind three polycarbonate panels with an RGB fan on top. The result is unique, and it is backed by a genuinely modern feature set, with ATX 3.1 compliance, full iCUE support, an integrated iCUE LINK System Hub, and a native 12V-2x6 connector with PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring. The latter is more than a bullet point on the box, as the unit shut down instantly when we pulled 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector.

It has been revealed that most importantly, the looks did not come at the expense of performance. The efficiency is excellent, with averages of 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC, and it barely moved when we raised the ambient temperature to 45°C. Voltage regulation is tight on every rail, and the ripple suppression is excellent, leaving a large margin against the ATX limits. At room temperature, the fan does not even spin up before the load reaches 500W and it stays quiet all the way up to the maximum output.

The compromises are few, but some of them are hard to ignore on a unit like this. The capacitors are all made by Elite and rebranded as Corsair. Elite is a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, but its capacitors are not something we frequently encounter above the mid-tier, and they are not a great match for a premium unit when the regular HX1000i SHIFT advertises Japanese capacitors. The fan uses a rifle bearing with a magnetic shaft instead of a fluid dynamic bearing, and it becomes loud under heavy load in a hot environment. The bundle is also spartan for an aesthetics-focused premium product. Finally, the 200 mm long chassis and the side-mounted connectors mean that not every case will accommodate the unit, although most buyers are likely to pair it with Corsair's matching 4500X case anyway. On the bright side, the ten-year warranty covers the unit for a period that very few users will ever need, and it makes the component choices easier to accept.

At the time of this review, Corsair had not made the price of the HX1000i Shift Crystal public, which makes a definitive value judgment impossible. The regular HX1000i SHIFT is the obvious comparison, as it offers the same side connector layout, iCUE integration, and iCUE LINK hub for $339.99 at Corsair's own store, along with a fluid dynamic bearing fan and Japanese capacitors. Compared to other showy high-end units, such as the Asus ROG Thor 1000W Platinum II or the Lian Li Edge 1000, the CRYSTAL is the only one that actually puts its internals on display, and its Cybenetics Platinum efficiency and tight electrical performance mean that it does not need its looks to justify itself. If it arrives at a reasonable premium over the regular HX1000i SHIFT, it is an easy recommendation for anyone building a showcase system, and a well-performing 1000W unit for everyone else who simply likes how it looks, as long as they can live with its parts selection.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google just pulled a fast one on the calendar by releasing Android 17 QPR2 a month early.
  • According to recent reports, the enhancement, shared by Google's Mishaal Rahman on Reddit, comes after a lengthy beta period, and while some of the changes are currently exclusive to Pixel devices, others may eventually be coming to phones from other Android manufacturers.
  • One of the more apparent changes is a more robust color customization system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google just pulled a fast one on the calendar by releasing Android 17 QPR2 a month early. Riding shotgun with the November Pixel Drop, the patch is rolling out to supported Pixel devices, from the budget-friendly Pixel 6a to the latest hardware.

According to recent reports, the enhancement, shared by Google's Mishaal Rahman on Reddit, comes after a lengthy beta period, and while some of the changes are currently exclusive to Pixel devices, others may eventually be coming to phones from other Android manufacturers. There’s more than just more bug fixes here, especially if you like to have control over how your phone looks and behaves.

One of the more apparent changes is a more robust color customization system. Customers don't have to stick with Google's preset color schemes anymore but instead can bring up a rainbow hue slider and pick a custom system color. There are also four intensity options: Neutral, Soft, Bright, and Bold.

According to recent reports, google is also introducing adaptive light and dark wallpaper support. Compatible wallpaper collections can automatically switch between light and dark versions of their wallpapers depending on the system theme.

Google is giving users more control of the status bar. There’s a new settings page to select whether to show all notification icons, priority notifications only, or none. You can also hide individual system indicators like battery percentage, mute, and vibration.

Another welcome adjustment is the brightness controls. Previously, some apps could lock screen brightness at maximum, preventing people from reducing screen brightness through Quick Settings. QPR2 removes that restriction so you can change the brightness even if an app overrides the setting.

Bluetooth LE Audio gets a major upgrade with the addition of a fresh Voice Broadcast feature. Users can broadcast their voice using the phone’s microphone or a connected wired headset, with nearby listeners tuning in using compatible Auracast headphones, hearing devices, or Android phones. You can also password protect private broadcasts.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Google is improving Auracast discovery with QR codes, NFC tap-to-join, and a dedicated Quick Settings tile. Compatible devices can also make broadcasts easier to follow with Live Caption and Translation.

Foldable owners also get a new handle at the top of app windows, making it easier to move between full-screen apps, split-screen layouts, and floating bubbles.

Recent findings suggest that security-wise, Android has a cleaner app-install dialog, letting you choose between temporary or permanent permission options for sideloading. It also prevents some risky actions during calls from unknown contacts, such as enabling Developer options, and asks you to confirm before executing call-forwarding codes.

There’s also a new Private Compute Core logging option that lets customers see data shared with on-device AI features.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the Linux Terminal app now supports guest-to-host file sharing. The Android file manager will let users manage the Linux virtual machine files and browse, edit, and move them.

Android 17 QPR2 also brings accessibility improvements, lets you customize the keyboard’s vibration, offers better hearing-device controls, and adds an option for a home time zone.

Make sure to opt out of the Android Beta Program first if you want the stable OTA build without wiping your storage. Pixel owners can pull down the over-the-air update from system settings right now, while non-Pixel owners will need to wait for their respective manufacturers to adapt the codebase.

But hours before this move, when it was just rumored that the Nvidia board was planning to oust him, Elon Musk had already stated his willingness to hire the former Nvidia chief on X. @zerohedge That would be an honorNovember 12, 2026.

Despite the scandals that Jensen is currently facing, he still has the engineering know-how, deep knowledge of the industry and its inner workings, plus multiple connections across the world, which would be extremely valuable for any manufacturer looking to break into the semiconductor industry.

This is exactly what Elon Musk is doing with his Terafab project, which he first mentioned in November 2025. Jensen Huang even warned that this was going to be a challenge, pointing out that “the engineering, the science, and the artistry of doing what TSMC does for a living is extremely hard.” Nevertheless, Musk poured his resources into the project, with construction on the Terafab facility in full swing and with plans to hit volume chip production by the second half of 2028. Musk himself noted that the site targets a production capacity of a million wafers a month by 2032. Tesla has an ambitious AI accelerator roadmap, and SpaceX has even touted making its own GPUs in the future.

We still don’t know what Jensen Huang’s intends are, but even though he’s no longer a part of the Nvidia board and its leadership, Jensen and his wife, Lori, still jointly own approximately 800 million Nvidia shares through various trusts and LLCs, while Huang himself personally owns around 70 million Nvidia shares.

Aside from that, he still has an outstanding invitation from Congress to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols, which could turn into a subpoena if he snubs them, although we don’t know how his resignation would affect the closed-door meeting. There’s also a reported FBI investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive who was allegedly instrumental in the import of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China and is suspected of working with China’s Ministry of State Security.

According to recent reports, jensen Huang is just the latest in the long list of executives who resigned or were ousted from their leadership position because of a relationship or an affair with a subordinate. This includes former Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher in 2005, HP CEO Mark Hurd in 2010, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in 2018, and former McDonald’s CEO Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Musk himself is known to have had relationships with subordinates from his various companies, and that he has even fathered four children with Shivon Zilis, a top executive at Neuralink who started working at Tesla in 2017, through IVF.

It’s still not confirmed if Musk’s reply is a serious offer for Jensen Huang. But if the former Nvidia chief ever decides to work for Musk on his Terafab project, then Jensen could put his effort and expertise into turning it into a formidable competitor to Nvidia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in my role as TechRadar's Senior Fitness and Wearables Editor, I test a lot of smartwatches and fitness trackers. I've tested around a dozen wrist-based fitness trackers this year alone, and what I haven't tested, I've asked other writers to put through their paces for me.

My personal testing bank this year includes the following:.

The devices that other writers have tested on my behalf include the Garmin Forerunner 70, Samsung Galaxy Watch 9, Amazfit Active 3 Premium, Coros Nomad, Suunto Race 3s, Huawei Band 11 and many more. Then there are the items from previous years, as well as devices such as heart rate monitors and smart rings. Over the years, I've tested a lot of smartwatches and fitness tech, and I'm well placed to advise on which Black Friday smartwatch deals to consider.

So, some readers might be surprised when I say that my advice to the majority is to give most of the above trackers a wide berth on Black Friday, with the possible exception of the Google Fitbit Air and Garmin Cirqa.

Most smartwatches, like smartphones, work on churn: every one to two years, a company will release a newer model of the same watch, with a few newly introduced features and perhaps a minor tweak to the design. It's keeps their watch lines up to date, delivering the best-in-class health metrics for buyers, while ensuring that the range regularly stays level with the competition, rather than becoming outdated and requiring a total overhaul. Technology moves swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that for example, this year saw Apple deliver new Siri AI features and a more accurate, redesigned LED sensor array to the Watch, which better detects your heart rate overnight. Wear the Watch overnight and it will give you a Readiness Score the next day, which tells you how much energy you're likely to have in the tank for the day ahead. This can aid in planning your training sessions, and help you tailor your habits to ensure maximum Readiness when you need it.

These features aren't available on the older watches — but previous models do include everything else. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 look and operate the same as the Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra 3, bar a few other quality-of-life fixes, making them an excellent buy on Black Friday. And retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy in the US, and Argos in the UK will be offering significant discounts to clear old stock.

Recent findings suggest that the Garmin Forerunner 170 isn't likely to see much movement in price, but its predecessor, the Garmin Forerunner 165 will see larger discounts. The Forerunner 165 includes the same Elevate V4 heart rate sensing technology embedded in its case, so it's the design, features and software support that are slightly different in the models rather than any accuracy gains.

The same is true of last year's edition of the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra and the Google Pixel Watch 4, both of which were released in 2025: their 2026 successors are iterative updates on these watches. If the price cut is significant on those older models (and it's already the case on the Samsung model below), you should probably buy the older model instead of the newer one.

In a recent development, we loved the device in our Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra review, praising its tough exterior, user interface and its awesome range of features. However, we did note that the screen is the exact same size as the less expensive Galaxy Watch 7’s and we'd have preferred a bigger battery. That said, if you’re an athletic person looking for an Android-based smartwatch, the Galaxy Watch Ultra is one of your best options.

The same is also true of the Garmin Fenix range: the all-newly introduced Garmin Fenix 9 might be super expensive, but the Fenix 8 from 2024 has already dropped significantly in price:.

According to recent reports, save 24% on the stellar Garmin Fenix 8 in its 47mm size. I rated this watch five stars, calling it "rugged, expensive perfection" in my Garmin Fenix 8 review.

Next year, I'm sure I'll be offering the same advice, but with devices replaced by this year's models instead — it's the nature of consumer technology.

Industry observers note that if you're interested in getting yourself a newly introduced smartwatch or fitness tracker, look at the previous iteration of a product instead of the latest tech. The cycle of small upgrades rather than giant overhauls means that older tech is still plenty good enough for most people's needs — and it's more wallet-friendly, too.

Of this year's crop of devices, the models I recommend picking up are the Google Fitbit Air and the Garmin Cirqa.

Recent findings suggest that why? Simply because they're first-generation devices, so there aren't any historic discounts on older models to be found. In addition, they're unlikely to see a refresh for a couple of years at least — certainly not annually, on account of their limited feature set, the nature of screenless trackers, and the fact that they're both fairly high-quality pieces of kit worthy of a space on your wrist. In particular, the Garmin Cirqa is my pick for one of the best fitness trackers this year. If you see a discount on either, I'd advise you grab one.

Are you getting a newly introduced wearable in the Black Friday sales this year? Let us know in the comments.
